en: The *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*, Fascicle Three:

Regarding the "Chapter on Antidotes" (*Pratipakṣa-paṭala*), it is so named because it investigates and practices the path of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and elucidates their respective meanings according to the specific [defilements] they counteract. Within this, the meaning is first clarified, and subsequently...

Exegesis of the Text. Regarding the meaning of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), there are briefly six sections: first, the enumeration of their names; second, the explanation of their meanings;

third, the determination of their essential natures (*svabhāva*); fourth, the clarification of their stages and levels (*bhūmi*); fifth, the exposition of their sequence; and sixth, the analysis of their various categories.
First, regarding the enumeration of names: what are the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*)? They are:

the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness: first, the foundation of mindfulness on the body; second, the foundation of mindfulness on feelings; third, the foundation of mindfulness on the mind; and fourth, the foundation of mindfulness on phenomena. The four right...

Regarding "abandonment": first, for the sake of abandoning evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, one generates desire, exerts oneself, arouses diligence, and applies right effort to uplift and sustain the mind;
second, for the sake of preventing evil and unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising.

1. One generates desire, exerts effort, and so forth, up to maintaining the mind through right abandonment, for the sake of abandoning unwholesome states that have already arisen. 2. One generates desire, exerts effort, and so forth, up to maintaining the mind through right abandonment, for the sake of preventing unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising. 3.

One generates desire, exerts effort, and so forth, up to maintaining the mind through right abandonment, for the sake of causing wholesome states that have not yet arisen to arise. 4. One generates desire, exerts effort, and so forth, up to maintaining the mind through right abandonment, for the sake of maintaining wholesome states that have already arisen.
To cause them not to be forgotten; to cause them to be cultivated to perfection; to cause them to be practiced more intensely; to cause them to increase; and to cause them to become vast.

One generates desire and exerts effort, up to the right abandonment of maintaining the mind. As for the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): first, the base of psychic power consisting of the accomplishment of the mental formation of concentration through desire;

second, the base of psychic power consisting of the accomplishment of the mental formation of concentration through exertion; third, the base of psychic power consisting of the mental formation of concentration through the mind... [and so forth].

The basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration through the exercise of volition; the basis of psychic power consisting in the accomplishment of concentration through the exercise of investigation.

The five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*) are: first, the faculty of faith; second, the faculty of energy; third, the faculty of mindfulness; fourth, the faculty of concentration; fifth, the faculty of wisdom. The five powers (*pañcabalāni*) are:

the power of faith, up to the power of wisdom. The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅgāni*) are: first, the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness; second, the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena; third, the factor of enlightenment that is energy...

The factors of enlightenment: fourth, the factor of enlightenment of joy; fifth, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility; sixth, the factor of enlightenment of concentration; seventh, the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
As for the eightfold noble path: first, right view; second, right intention; third, right speech; fourth, right action; fifth, right livelihood; sixth, right effort;
seventh, right mindfulness; eighth, right concentration.

The second [section] explains the meaning. That is to say, dwelling in association with mindfulness regarding the body and cultivating the contemplation of the body is the "mindfulness of the body" (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

This is stated in the same way for everything up to the "dharmas. What is mindfulness? It refers to the upholding of the true Dharma by taking the body as the primary basis, reflecting upon the meaning of the Dharma, and practicing its realization.
Regarding both the words and their meaning, and within the practice of realization, the mind does not forget.
Because it is lost. What is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*)? It refers to the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation based upon the body as the predominant condition.
By means of this wisdom, one correctly contemplates and correctly investigates all aspects of the entire body, because one contemplates accordingly and realizes accordingly.
How does one cultivate contemplation? Either "following the body" or "cultivating the body. Regarding "following the body": it means following the substantial body to contemplate its reflection.
The image-body is called "contemplation of the body according to the body," as explained in the Abhidharma. How does one contemplate the body according to the body?

It means discerning the distinct reflected image-body as being equal to the actual body; because one contemplates the object of the body and contemplates its similarity to the body, it is called "contemplation of the body according to the body.
By means of the gateway of contemplating the reflected image-body, one observes with thorough scrutiny.

Because it is the essential body (*svabhāvakāya*). To say "one cultivates the contemplation" means it has the sense of "revolving. This does not mean merely contemplating the body of marks (*lakṣaṇakāya*);
rather, within that, one further contemplates the body of suchness (*tathatākāya*). As stated in the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:

"How does a bodhisattva dwell in the cultivation of the contemplation of the body? It is by cultivating the revolving contemplation of the body of suchness upon the body of marks. How is mindfulness [cultivated]?
He dwells for the sake of guarding mindfulness, for the sake of being unstained by objects, and for the sake of abiding securely in the focal object.
Regarding "guarding mindfulness," it is said that he first guards mindfulness. Regarding "being unstained by objects through constant and careful mindfulness," it refers to what is said:

mindfulness guards the mind as it moves, comes, and so forth, whether dwelling or not dwelling; it grasps the general characteristics (*nimitta*) but does not grasp the secondary details (*anuvyañjana*). This is explained at length.

...up to: "guarding the faculty of the mind and practicing restraint for the sake of abiding in the object of focus. This means that as it is said, one establishes mindfulness upon the four objects of focus (*ālambana*).

Because of these three characteristics, one dwells well in mindfulness; therefore, it is called *smṛty-upasthāna* (application of mindfulness) and also *smṛty-upasthāna* (establishment of mindfulness).
"Upasthāna" has the meaning of "abiding. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "Mindfulness accords with wisdom and abides correctly within the object. This is [the definition].

It is called "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*). To speak generally: both that which is the foundation of mindfulness and that by means of which one dwells in mindfulness are termed "foundations of mindfulness.

Regarding "that which is the foundation of mindfulness," this refers to the foundation of mindfulness as the object (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding "that by means of which one dwells in mindfulness," this refers to either wisdom (*prajñā*) or mindfulness (*smṛti*) that sustains meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

these constitute the foundational mindfulness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*). All other associated mental states and mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) are the [foundations of mindfulness] of concomitance (*sahāya*).

One should practice the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). This is as explained in the *Śrutamayībhūmi*. This is called a brief explanation of the meaning of the foundations of mindfulness.

Next, to clarify the meaning of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*): what are "evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen"? They refer to those capable of giving rise to unwholesome conduct.
The afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), which are comprised within the coarse entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), are termed "already arisen.

"For the sake of their abandonment" means cultivating the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) so that they become attenuated. "Generating the desire" means giving rise to the aspiration for realization and abandonment.
"Exerting oneself" means not tolerating evil and turning toward abandonment. "Arousing diligent effort" refers to [the practice] in its many forms.

"Steadfast. This refers to cultivating those remedies. These three preceding phrases clarify that within the non-concentrated states (*asamāhita-bhūmi*), both the wisdoms of hearing and reflection constitute a lower-grade remedy for rousing the mind;
that is, one cultivates those remedies and brings the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) into manifestation. If the mind becomes sunken (*laya*), [one applies this remedy].
When the mind is afflicted by the defilements of the *kleśas*, one applies effort to uplift it;

thus, "holding the mind" refers to the time when this very antidote is being practiced, and if the mind becomes agitated or uplifted and is stained by the *kleśas*, one holds the mind to cause it to descend. What are the "unarisen evil and unwholesome states"?

They are called "unarisen" because they consist of the causes capable of giving rise to coarse entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), which are comprised within the intensified latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Regarding "because they do not arise": it is for the purpose of ensuring that coarse entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) do not manifest. "Generating desire" refers to the arising of the wish to realize their non-manifestation.
"Exerting effort" refers to dwelling in non-forgetfulness, so as to remain well-established in mindfulness (*smṛti*) to prevent them from manifesting.
The following four phrases are as previously explained. What are "wholesome dharmas not yet arisen"?

They refer to the three types of wisdom—arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation—which are called "wholesome dharmas" because they are free from fault. That which has not yet been attained is called "not yet arisen.
"Arousing desire for their arising" means generating the desire for their realization. "Exerting effort" means seeking the correct means for their acquisition.
Therefore, "arousing right effort" means practicing for a long duration with earnestness, frequently and firmly.

These three preceding phrases clarify the wholesome dharmas subsumed under the two types of wisdom—listening and reflection—which belong to the non-concentrated stages (*asamāhita-bhūmi*). "Exerting the mind and sustaining the mind" is for the sake of attaining the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*);

the rest is as explained previously. What are the "wholesome dharmas already arisen"? They are so called because they have already been attained. Regarding "establishing mindfulness": [it is for the sake of maintaining them].
That which is called "hearing-wisdom" (śrutamayī-prajñā) causes one not to forget; that which is called "reflection-wisdom" (cintāmayī-prajñā) causes one to fulfill cultivation;
that which is called "cultivation-wisdom" (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā) causes one to bring it to completion. These three preceding phrases clarify that one merely guards what has already been attained.

As for the phrase "causing the cultivated goodness to be practiced doubly, to increase, and to expand," these correspond respectively to the fact that one does not merely give rise to contentment with that [attainment]. The phrases concerning the arising of desire and so forth are all as previously explained. This...
The meaning is as explained at length in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*. Regarding "right abandonment" (*samyak-prahāṇa*), it is also called "right exertion" (*samyak-vyāyāma*).

"Exertion" (*vyāyāma*) is the name for its essential nature (*svabhāva*), while "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*) is a designation for its function (*karman*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because one destroys all erroneous dharmas and proceeds upon the right path, it is called 'right exertion'."

Regarding "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*), one should understand the explanation given in the *Yogācārabhūmi*. The first is called "abandonment through restraint" (*saṃvara-prahāṇa*); the second is called "abandonment by abandonment" (*prahāṇa-prahāṇa*).

Because one should cultivate restraint regarding evil and unwholesome states that have already arisen, so as to cause them to be extinguished and not tolerate them, it is called "abandonment through restraint.
Regarding evil states that have not yet arisen, one causes them not to manifest; because one abandons them so that they do not appear before one, it is called "abandonment by abandonment."

The first is called abandonment through abandonment (*prahāṇa-prahāṇa*). The third is called abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*). The fourth is called abandonment through protection (*anurakṣaṇā-prahāṇa*).

Because one repeatedly cultivates and practices wholesome dharmas, those not previously attained are certainly brought into manifestation, and that which was to be abandoned is effectively abandoned; therefore, it is called abandonment through cultivation.
Because one remains free from negligence regarding the wholesome dharmas already attained, practicing them to perfection, one protects what has already arisen and is able to [prevent its loss].

Because they are to be abandoned, they are called "abandonment through guarding. In brief, in order to demonstrate the perfection of the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) and the perfection of the application (*prayoga*) regarding the acts of relinquishing and adopting within the categories of the black and white sides, four kinds of right exertions (*samyakprahāṇa*) are taught.
It should be understood that herein, the perfection of the intention arises from the production of desire, and [the perfection of application] from self-exertion, up to...

Because of maintaining the mind, the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is perfected. What has been explained above is extracted from the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*; this is called the brief explanation of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Regarding the meaning of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): why are they called the four kinds—desire, exertion, mind, and investigation?
There are two meanings [to this]: either these four factors are present in a single person, or they are predominant in different individuals respectively.
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 98, states: "Furthermore, by means of four kinds of powers, one sustains the mind and brings it to concentration;
therefore, the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are established. What are the four? First, the power of pure intention (*āśaya*); second, the power of diligent application (*vyāyāma*)."
Third is the power of joy and delight; fourth is the power of the correct knowledges (*samyakprahāṇa*).
It should be understood that herein, by means of the first power, one generates the desire for concentration (*samādhi*) so as to realize it, and applies diligent effort.

By means of the second power, one initially settles the mind and causes it to become stable. By means of the third power, once the mind is settled in concentration, it no longer becomes distracted, nor does one...

I further drift and turn again by means of the fourth power: I observe meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and, regarding the afflictions to be countered, I know as they truly are whether they have been abandoned or not yet abandoned.
Furthermore, I am able to skillfully discern the characteristics of entering, abiding in, and emerging from meditative absorption.
Likewise, regarding all the characteristics of *śamatha* and so forth, as well as the secondary afflictions associated with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and their respective antidotes—
He knows them all as they truly are. Regarding "one who delights in concentration," within that concentration there is only the functional activity of such concentration;
beyond this, there is nothing further, neither exceeding nor adding to it. This passage demonstrates that a practitioner of one aspect possesses four kinds of power to achieve concentration;
therefore, the four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) are established. How does each individual [practitioner] follow one [aspect]?
Regarding "predominance," as stated in the *Śāsanodbhāvana-śāstra* (*Xianyang lun*):

"One who attains samādhi through the predominance of desire" refers to a practitioner who, in previous lives, cultivated superior roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) in the presence of a Great Teacher or among wise fellow-practitioners.

One generates faith and generates desire. One listens to the sublime Dharma. Having heard the sublime Dharma according to what one has faith in and delights in, one successively realizes one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
Through this desire, meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is accomplished. "Accomplishment" means that within this state, one attains mastery.
Second, regarding the attainment of meditative concentration through the predominance of diligence (*vīrya*): it is as when a practitioner...
Relying upon the methods of instruction and admonition, whether in a secluded place, among the trees of a forest, or in a quiet chamber,
one applies oneself with long-term vigor, thorough mastery, and fervor in such locations to realize one-pointedness of mind through right effort;
by means of that right effort, samādhi is accomplished, for it is through the predominance of the third mental state that samādhi is attained.
As for this: suppose there is a practitioner who has previously cultivated the practice of *śamatha*.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, they contemplate internal phenomena and swiftly realizes the one-pointedness of mind. Through the cultivation of the mind, *samādhi* is accomplished.
Regarding the attainment of *samādhi* through the predominance of the fourth contemplation: suppose there is a practitioner who is widely learned and retains what they have heard; their learning...

Having accumulated [merit], dwelling alone in the joy of tranquility, one discriminates those very phenomena with wisdom—discriminating them most subtly, fully awakening to them, and investigating them.
Through this, one realizes the one-pointedness of mind; through such investigation, samādhi is accomplished.
This passage demonstrates that one who relies on the four applications of mental effort (*catur-ṛddhipāda*) achieves meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through the predominance of any one of them;

therefore, four types of bases for psychic power are established. Regarding the statement that "in all four, the application of mental effort is accomplished," the eight types of application of mental effort will be explained in detail later.
As for the term "bases for psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*), it is established by way of analogy, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*: "Just as one who has feet is able to go and..."
Returning, leaping, and being courageous and vigorous, one is able to attain the sublime dharmas of the world. These sublime worldly dharmas are called "divine" (*ṛddhi*).
Because one can reach these, they are called "bases of divine power" (*ṛddhipāda*).

Likewise, if there are various dharmas such as desire and so forth, and one possesses samādhi that is perfected, accomplished, capable, and unshakable, one is able to go and return, leaping and being courageous and vigorous.

"Vīrya" (diligence) means being able to attain and realize the supramundane, supreme dharmas. Because one attains the most excellent mastery through these supramundane dharmas, it is called the "supreme *ṛddhi*" (power).
Because one can realize this, it is named "*ṛddhipāda*" (basis of power). This is also called the "basis of [wishes as] desired" (*cetanā-ṛddhipāda*). "Pāda" means fulfillment;

because it fulfills what is wished for, it is called the "basis of [wishes as] desired. Furthermore, it refers to feet, because they enable one to go somewhere. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Question:

At the time of the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*), because the mind is slightly distracted, one gathers the mind through concentration; thus, there are the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhi-pāda*).
It is, for example, like fine food that lacks flavor when salt is insufficient, but whose flavor becomes perfect and as desired once salt is obtained.

Or again, it is like a person who has two feet and further obtains a fine horse or a fine carriage, reaching wherever they wish. The practitioner is likewise: having obtained the true wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*), [they proceed].

Right effort is the central application of diligence. Because of this diligence, wisdom increases while the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) remains weak; thus, one attains the four kinds of concentration.
By means of the concentrated mind, wisdom and the power of concentration become equal, whereby all that is wished for is attained; therefore, they are called the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the bases of psychic power. Regarding the meaning of the five faculties (*indriya*): the sense of "predominance" (*ādhipatya*) is the meaning of "faculty. That is to say, regarding the ability to...
They give rise to supramundane dharmas because faith and the other [faculties] serve as their predominant conditions (*adhipati*).

Furthermore, each preceding faculty serves as the predominant condition for the arising of each subsequent dharma, continuing until the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), which relates exclusively to the supramundane.

This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Regarding the meaning of the five powers (*pañcabala*): the meaning of "power" is the sense of being difficult to subdue. That is to say, even if a celestial Māra...

If there are no śramaṇas, brahmins, or others in the world who can rightfully lead them astray or overpower them, and even the afflictions cannot bend them, they are therefore called "difficult to subdue.
By virtue of these powers, they possess great majesty and authority;
they crush the forces of all māra-armies and are able to realize the permanent exhaustion of all outflows (āsravas). For this reason, they are called "powers" (bala). This is...
This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the five powers (*pañca-balāni*). Regarding the meaning of these faculties (*indriya*) and powers, it is explained according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

As for the meaning of the seven factors of enlightenment (*sapta-bodhyaṅgāni*): they are the wisdom of realization as it truly is (*yathābhūta-abhisamaya-prajñā*) belonging to those individuals (*pudgala*) who have already entered into the state of rightness and departure from birth (*samyaktva-nyāma*).

Because this serves as their constituent part (*aṅga*), they are called "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhyaṅga*). They are also called "limbs of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*). The term "part" (*pakṣa*) signifies a cause; because they are able to attain the fruit of enlightenment, they are called "enlightenment."

[The term] *aṅga* (limb/factor) is as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: because these seven things can reach the ultimate through the true wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they are called "limbs.
This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). Regarding the meaning of the Eightfold Noble Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*):

those noble ones in training (*śaikṣa*) who have already seen the track [of the Dharma], by means of the practice-path and the right path subsumed within these eight limbs, are able to sever all afflictions (*kleśa*) without remainder and are able to [attain] liberation...
One realizes liberation to its ultimate conclusion; therefore, it is called the Noble Eightfold Path, and it is also called the Right Path (*samyag-mārga*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Because one wishes to enter the city of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nirvāṇa, one practices these various dharmas; at that time, it is called the Right Path. This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the Right Path.
Question: Are not all seven of these factors correct? Why is it that the Path of Exertion (*vyāyāma-mārga*) alone is singled out [as the Right Path]?

Regarding the attainment of the correct name: the answer is as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. There are four kinds of diligence (*vīrya*); because the mind is stirred with courage and one fears error, it is called "right effort" (*samyak-vyāyāma*).
Furthermore, when practicing the path, because one fears falling into a wrong path, it is called the "right path" (*samyak-mārga*).
The distinctions within these shall also be explained later. This is a brief explanation of the meaning of the eight factors of the path (*aṣṭāṅga-mārga*).

Third, regarding the elucidation of their essential nature (*svabhāva*): they are established through their functions, totaling thirty-seven. However, when their essential nature is examined, they do not exceed ten dharmas, namely:

ethical discipline (*śīla*), volition (*cetanā*), sensation (*vedanā*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), diligence (*vīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Among these, ethical discipline is comprised within the dharmas of manifest and unmanifest form (*vijñapti-avijñapti-rūpa*). The remaining nine are all comprised within mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). Among those, volition and sensation are included within the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

Second: mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are three among the specific objects (*viśeṣa-bhūmika*); diligence, faith, tranquility, and equanimity belong to the great wholesome ground (*kuśala-mahābhūmika*).

Based on these ten factors, the thirty-seven [limbs of enlightenment] are established: the precepts are divided into three—right speech, right action, and right livelihood; volition (*cetanā*) is established as one, namely right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*);

feeling (*vedanā*) is also established as one, namely the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*); and mindfulness is divided into four, namely the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), and the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Right Mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Eight factors are established for concentration (*samādhi*): namely, the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*).

Wisdom (*prajñā*) is also established as eight: namely, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), the power of wisdom (*prajñābala*), the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasambodhyaṅga*), and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

Diligence (*vīrya*) is also established as eight: namely, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*), the power of diligence (*vīryabala*), the factor of enlightenment of diligence (*vīryasambodhyaṅga*), and right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*). Faith (*śraddhā*)... [is also established as eight].

The two neutral factors are the faculty of faith and the power of faith. The factors of tranquility and equanimity each constitute one category, namely the awakening factor of tranquility and the awakening factor of equanimity.
In summary, there are five categories: first, opening the eight [factors] into three, namely concentration, wisdom, and diligence;
second, opening the four [factors] into one, namely mindfulness; third, opening the three [factors] into one, namely ethical discipline; fourth, opening the two [factors] into one, namely...
Faith. Of these five, there is only one [that remains as such], while four others consist of vitarka (thinking), vicāra (sustained thought), praśrabdhi (tranquility), and upekṣā (equanimity).
Within the first category, there are twenty-four; within the latter four categories, there are thirteen in total. Altogether, there are thirty-seven.

The reason for this variation in expansion and contraction is that because the power of concentration, wisdom, diligence, and progressive cultivation is great, they are expanded into eight; whereas vitarka, vicāra, and praśrabdhi remain as they are.
Because the power of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) is diminished when abandoned, each is established individually;

yet, since the power of the dharmas such as faith is included therein, four, three, and two are established according to the descending stages. Therefore, the essential nature consists of only ten dharmas. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The thirty-seven factors have ten dharmas as their basis," and so forth, as explained at length.
Fourth, regarding the clarification of the stages (*bhūmi*): if one examines their actual practice, they all pertain to every stage, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Furthermore, the wholesome, contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths that arise through the predominance of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena are all termed "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Moreover, the subsequent text states: "Briefly stated, all noble paths of persons are subsumed under two locations: first, the mundane; second, the supramundane."
Regarding the mundane: that which is mundane is so called because it is bound and fettered by the three outflows (*āsrava*) and the four graspings (*upādāna*), and thus cannot exhaust suffering.
Because it is of a wholesome nature (*kuśala-dharma*), it can lead to rebirth in the happy realms (*sugati*). The supramundane is the opposite of that; it can exhaust all sufferings.

Since the first and last of these two categories of phenomena have been explained in this way, one should know that the five intermediate phenomena are likewise so. Although they are common to all practice (*caryā*), they are distinguished according to their stages (*avasthā*).
They are established separately. What is the meaning of this? The stages (*bhūmi*) are largely divided and determined as two positions:

namely, the first five dharmas reside in the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the latter two dharmas are established within the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*). Regarding the five dharmas of the ordinary stage, there are two interpretations for their establishment.

These designations are established as appropriate and each possesses its own logical basis. Regarding the two dharmas of the noble stages, there are three reasons for their establishment. First, as in the *Abhidharmakośa*:

The treatise discusses another point, stating: Other masters say that the sequence is not disrupted, because one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and cultivates the factors of the noble path (*āryamārgāṅga*) within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) following the path of seeing. As for the second interpretation, it is as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

It is called "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) because it functions as the path of cultivation; it is called the "path" (*mārga*) because it functions as the path of seeing. The Vaibhāṣika masters also maintain this same view. As that treatise states:

According to their numerical order, there are first seven and then eight. This is the third meaning, as explained in this treatise.
The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) pertain to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while the path factors (*mārgāṅga*) pertain to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

This is also stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Thus, all three interpretations are logical; since they are established according to their respective meanings, there is nothing inappropriate about them.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains these three meanings in general. Its sixty-second fascicle states: "That which understands intrinsic nature refers to the Noble Eightfold Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). It further explains that this serves as an antidote (*pratipakṣa*).

The three aggregates are established because of the three types of affliction (*saṃkleśa*): namely, as the antidotes to the affliction of misconduct, the affliction of sensual desires, and the affliction of views.

This passage should be understood according to the first master’s explanation, for that which remedies views pertains to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while that which remedies sensual desires pertains to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). As stated in the eighteenth fascicle:
What is meant by "upright"? It refers to the arising of that noble eightfold path which flows against the current and is upright;

it is capable of severing all afflictions to be abandoned through vision, and one attains entry into conformity with the path that flows against the current. This passage should be understood according to the second meaning.
The twenty-ninth fascicle states: "At that time, because he has for the first time attained the seven factors of enlightenment, he is called 'one who has first attained awakening.

Having seen the path of the Noble Truths, he eternally eradicates all afflictions to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya-kleśa*), and cultivates the elimination of afflictions to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya-kleśa*). This passage corresponds to the third meaning."
The fifth [section] clarifies the sequence. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: Question: One should first explain the Path (*mārga*).
Why is it that one practices the Path and only thereafter attains the various wholesome dharmas? It is like a person who first travels the road and only thereafter reaches their destination.

Why, then, is this inverted—first explaining the Foundations of Mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and later explaining the Noble Eightfold Path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*)? Answer: This is not inverted. Among the thirty-seven [auxiliaries of enlightenment],...

This chapter concerns the initial stage when one first desires to enter the Path; it is called the "Factor of Causality" (*nidāna*). For example, when a practitioner goes to a teacher to hear the Dharma, they first employ mindfulness to uphold this teaching;
at that time, it is called "Mindfulness-Application" (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Having sought the fruit from within the Dharma, one then exerts vigor;

at that time, it is called "Right Effort" (*samyakpradhāna*). Because of excessive vigor, the mind becomes scattered and coarse; to collect the mind and make it supple, it is therefore called "Concentration" (*samādhi*).

When the mind has become pliant through the bases of psychic power, the five faculties arise. Because the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is extremely profound and difficult to understand, one is able to believe in it by virtue of the faculty of faith;
this is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*). Not begrudging body or life, but seeking the principle with a single mind, is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).

Constantly recollecting this Path and not recollecting other matters is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). Gathering the mind within the Path is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).

Contemplating the true nature of the truths is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). When these five faculties increase and are able to obstruct the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called powers (*bala*).
Having attained these powers, one discerns the factors of the path (*mārgadharma*). There are two divisions and three [aspects]; regarding the three dharmas, there are three arisings.

Regarding the three dharmas, the lower mindfulness abides in two places, like a gatekeeper; this is called the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). Having attained these dharmas, one desires to enter *nirvāṇa*.
Because it is the city of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one practices these eight dharmas; this is called the Path (*mārga*). Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"In this context, one should know that at the stage of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one first binds the mind and places it upon the object of focus (*ālambana*); subsequently, one dwells with mindfulness established upon that object."

One diligently cultivates the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*). Having subsequently attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one then diligently applies the preparatory practice (*prayoga*) among the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) in order to bring that concentration to perfect fulfillment.

Once concentration is fulfilled, one relies on the faculties (*indriya*) such as faith to cultivate the preparatory practice in order to achieve dissociation from all signs (*nimitta*) and coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Within this preparatory practice, the faculties are of a lower grade, while the powers (*bala*) are of a superior grade. Thus it is.
Having completed the path of application (*prayoga-mārga*), one next attains the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and penetrates the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Having penetrated the limit of reality, one next cultivates the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), gradually proceeding until the realization of unexcelled bodhi (*anuttara-bodhi*) and attaining liberation from all obscurations.
Thus, the sequence described in these two treatises is explained according to the gate of successive numerical stages.
Sixth, regarding the analysis of the various categories: these seven factors each possess five categories, as explained in the *Abhidharma*.
Furthermore, all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), being without distinction, are established by means of these five categories:
namely, by way of their object (*ālambana*), their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their accompaniments (*sahāya*), their cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanā-phala*).
Regarding the objects of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): these are the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena—these four matters. They are:

the matter that is the basis of the self, the matter that is the enjoyment of the self, the matter that is the self's own essence, and the matter of the self's defilement and purification. For what reason are only these four objects established?
Because foolish ordinary beings, due to their inverted cognition, for the most part conceive of a self as depending upon the embodied physical form and as enjoying pleasure and pain.
Therefore, taking the apprehension of objects as their characteristic, they are defiled by greed and the like, and purified by faith and the like.
For this reason, one first correctly observes the true characteristics of phenomena; thus, these four are established as the objects of focus (*ālambana*). Although this is the general explanation:
Regarding the analysis therein: each of these four matters has three types—namely, internal, external, and both internal and external.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, six meanings are briefly explained: first, the matter of sentient beings within one's own continuum is the object of the internal body;

second, matter that is not of the category of sentient beings in the external world is the object of the external body; third, matter belonging to other sentient beings is the object of the internal-external body.
Regarding the object: when one takes this internal body as a condition and gives rise to thoughts of affection and longing, it is called "internal feeling.

The same applies to the internal mind and internal phenomena, as well as to external and both internal-and-external [phenomena]. Second, that which is comprised by the sense faculties (*indriya*)—appropriated matter (*upātta-rūpa*)—is the internal body;

that which is not comprised by the sense faculties—non-appropriated matter (*anupātta-rūpa*)—is the external body; and non-appropriated matter that is comprised by the sense faculties is both internal and external.
The body. Taking these three kinds as objects, there arise feelings, mind, and mental factors. According to their respective correspondence, they constitute three types:

first, the matter associated with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) within one’s own internal meditative states is the internal body; second, the matter associated with heaviness (*dausthulya*) within one’s own internal non-meditative states is the external body;
third, the matter associated with pliancy or heaviness belonging to others is the internal-external body. Taking these three kinds as objects...
The mental factors associated with the arising of perception are likewise categorized as three, as should be understood from what preceded.

This continues up to the sixth [stage], wherein within one's own body, the characteristics of hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and so forth constitute the internal body; the characteristics of the hair, body hair, and so forth of another's body constitute the external body.

Furthermore, the characteristics of the internal body—whether transformed or untransformed, such as the bluish discoloration (*vinīlaka*) and so forth—and the characteristics of the external body—whether transformed or untransformed, such as the bluish discoloration and so forth—[are likewise to be understood].
Characteristics, similar dharmic nature, and equal dharmic nature—these constitute the internal and external body. Taking these three objects as conditions, there arise sensation, mind, and dharmas;

according to their respective applications, they are likewise threefold. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the internal body is also explained through six meanings, which are largely the same as what was previously stated, with only minor differences.
Viewing those two collectively constitutes the internal and external body; there is no distinction between internal and external. The former two...

It is not included. As it is said there: "Furthermore, one forms this thought: 'I did not find [the object] through internal contemplation; perhaps it exists externally? Yet, external contemplation likewise does not find it.

One thinks to oneself: 'Perhaps I am mistaken. Therefore, I shall now contemplate both internally and externally together. Contemplating the internal and contemplating the external separately is the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*);
contemplating them simultaneously is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Through both general and specific contemplation, [one realizes that it is] completely non-existent..."

This can be understood. Having completed the observation [of form], regarding feeling, mind, and phenomena, there are three categories: internal, external, and so forth. There are both common analogies and alternative explanations.

What are these alternative explanations? They state that feeling associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is internal feeling, while feeling associated with the five sensory consciousnesses is external feeling, and so forth.

Furthermore, a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*) is an internal mind, while a distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*) is an external mind, and so forth. This excludes feeling; the remaining mental factors are treated similarly.

The categories of phenomena such as these are internal phenomena; those that are dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are external phenomena, and so forth, as explained at length.

These constitute the objects of focus for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the second foundation of mindfulness, there are two meanings.
If considered in relation to that which is to be remedied, its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*), because it correctly remedies the four inversions (*viparyāsa*) through wisdom. If...

Regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*), its essence consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*). This is because wisdom and mindfulness both abide together upon the object of focus. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The wisdom that contemplates the body, up to the wisdom that contemplates phenomena (*dharma*), constitutes the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the foundations of mindfulness.

This explains the essential nature by way of contrast with that which is to be remedied. The *Pratipakṣa-śāstra* states: "The intrinsic substance of the foundations of mindfulness refers to wisdom and mindfulness," as it is taught in the Buddha’s sūtras.

Because there are instances where [the term] "contemplating" (*anupaśyanā*) is applied to the body and so forth, and because there is the expression "application of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*), these [terms] refer respectively to their objects and their intrinsic nature.

Regarding the third application of mindfulness, its attendants (*sahāya*) consist of the mental factors associated with it, as well as the results produced with it as the primary cause, as explained in the Abhidharma. As for the attendants of the applications of mindfulness, they are those associated with them...
"Corresponding mental states and mental factors," etc. "Those" refers to those two dharmas of mindfulness and wisdom. The *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) says:

"What is called the 'shared foundations of mindfulness' (*sādhāraṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*)? Taking the contemplation of the body as primary, the path produced through causes and conditions—whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)—is the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
This applies likewise up to the contemplation of dharmas. Furthermore, the text below states that within the shared foundations of mindfulness, [there are] body and speech...
The two karmas constitute form-phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*); the remainder are non-form because they are not material.
Regarding the cultivation of the fourth foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are briefly two approaches: namely, common cultivation and uncommon cultivation.

Common cultivation refers to practicing the contemplation of the body in accordance with the internal body and so forth, as well as the external body and both internal and external bodies, in common with the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
This refers to the contemplation of impurity up to non-self. Knowing these names, one understands that such practices are cultivated in common with the Hīnayāna.

As for uncommon cultivation, it is practiced by Bodhisattvas alone; that is, regarding the body and so forth, they eliminate the notions of internal and external, contemplating only the body and so forth as the Middle Way and true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).

As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, these bodhisattvas universally and correctly understand all the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) within the principles of both vehicles—that is, both the principles of the Śrāvaka vehicle and the principles of the Mahāyāna.

Regarding the body: he dwells in the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupaśyanā*). He does not conceptualize the existence of an intrinsic nature within the body, nor does he conceptualize that all categories of it are entirely non-existent.
Furthermore, regarding the body, he remains detached from verbal expression and understands its self-nature (*svabhāva*) and dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) as they truly are;
this is explained at length. It further says: moreover, the bodhisattva who diligently cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) based on emptiness briefly [contemplates] six...
Among these, one is bound by signs; [the teaching] causes the mind to be liberated from this bondage. What are the six? They are as follows:

regarding the body, and so on up to mental phenomena (*dharma*), one gives rise to an internal sign—this is the first bondage of signs. Within that very same context, one gives rise to an external sign—this is the second bondage.
Within that very same context, one gives rise to both internal and external signs—this is the third bondage. If, regarding the immeasurable beings in the ten directions...
"May they be liberated from their afflictions. To cultivate the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)—the various signs (*nimitta*) herein constitute the fourth bond.
If, by means of these, one dwells in contemplation regarding objects such as the body—the various signs herein constitute the fifth bond.
For one who dwells in contemplation regarding the body and so forth—the various signs herein constitute the sixth bond. This is explained at length, up to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
It is said: Regarding the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness, one contemplates this internal body as impermanent;
it is like a disease, like an abscess, a mass of calamities, subject to decay, filled with impurities, and from which the nine orifices flow. It is a walking latrine. To speak at length, up to:
this bodily form does not exist within, nor does it exist without, nor does it exist in between. This body’s prior limit and its posterior...
The past limit, the present limit, and the future limit are all unattainable. They arise merely from the conjunction of the causes and conditions of all phenomena.
Those causes and conditions that produce this body also exist due to false and inverted perceptions. Within these causes and conditions, there is no characteristic of causes and conditions.

These conditions that give rise [to it] also lack the characteristic of arising. Contemplating and investigating the characteristics in this way, one knows that this body has, from the very beginning, lacked the characteristic of arising.
Because there is no arising, there is no characteristic; because there is no characteristic, there is no arising. It is merely a deception of ordinary people that it is called a "body.
When a bodhisattva contemplates the true reality of the body in this manner, they become free from all defiled attachments and dwell with mindfulness fixed upon the body.

The contemplation of observing the body is called the Bodhisattva’s application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). Observing the external body and the internal-external body is likewise.

[This applies to] sensation, mind, and phenomena, as explained at length. Fifth, regarding the clarification of the fruit of cultivating the applications of mindfulness, it is as stated in the *Abhidharma*:

one abandons the four inversions, enters into the four truths, and attains dissociation from the body and so forth; this is called the fruit of cultivation, namely, the abandonment of the four [inversions].

Regarding "perversions": this refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). In their respective order, they are able to sever the four perversions of purity, pleasure, permanence, and self.

By means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body, one enters into the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), because all physical bodies are manifested as being characterized by the pervasive suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) and heavy dysfunction (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Therefore, when practicing meditative cultivation (*vipaśyanā*), this pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is able to counteract [the afflictions], as it arises with differentiation within the body.

Through the application of mindfulness to feelings (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), because various feelings such as pleasure are the basis for the conjunction of craving and so forth.

Through the application of mindfulness to the mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); by contemplating that consciousness is devoid of a self and will eventually become non-existent, one gives rise to fear regarding the gate of the annihilation of the self.

The fear of *nirvāṇa* is abandoned because of its eternal separation [from suffering]. Through the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one enters into the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) in order to abandon the factors to be countered (*vipakṣadharma*) and to cultivate the remedial factors (*pratipakṣadharma*).
Furthermore, these four [applications of mindfulness], according to their true sequence, are able to realize the fruit of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*) from body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
By practicing this, one is gradually able to distance oneself from the heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the body and so forth. This clarifies the distant [separation].

One is free from the heavy burdens (*dausthulya*) of the four bonds. Regarding these four bonds: first, the bond of appropriation (*upādāna-bandhana*); second, the bond of experience (*anubhava-bandhana*); third, the bond of discernment (*vijñapti-bandhana*);
and fourth, the bond of attachment (*abhiniveśa-bandhana*). By means of these four bonds, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) is bound.

This refers to the mind in relation to the body being bound by the bond of appropriation; that is, it appropriates the internal body and dwells within it with a sense of security. Because of this, one is unable to escape the afflictions associated with the body.
Furthermore, the mind is bound to feeling by the bond of experiencing; it is associated with feeling and conforms to suffering and pleasure.
Because it is thus unable to escape the affliction of feeling, the mind is bound to all sense objects by the bond of discernment, grasping at the six sense objects as its objective referents.

It does not abide at any time; because it is not free from the affliction of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the mind is bound by the bondage of attachment toward various doubts and is associated with those doubts.

Following after all phenomena, because it is not free from the fault of the afflictions (*kleśa*), one should know—as stated in the *Yogācāra*—that the mind is bound by the bondage of appropriation (*upādāna*) toward the body, and bound by the bondage of internal experience toward sensation (*vedanā*).
Bound by the bondage of discernment (*vijñapti-bandhana*) regarding the characteristics of objects such as form;
and bound by the bondage of attachment (*abhiniveśa-bandhana*) through great and small afflictions such as greed and hatred toward the aforementioned phenomena of the body and so forth.

In order to counteract these four kinds of bondage, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are established. This is the fruit of cultivating the foundations of mindfulness. A brief [explanation] of the five gates of the foundations of mindfulness follows.
Thus it is said.

Next, the five gates within the four right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) are explained. Regarding the objects of focus (*ālambana*) of the right abandonments: they consist of the factors to be abandoned (*heya*) and their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), whether already arisen or yet to arise.
The first right abandonment takes as its object factors to be abandoned that have already arisen. The second right abandonment takes as its object...
The first [right abandonment] takes as its object the unarisen factors to be abandoned. The third right abandonment takes as its object the unarisen remedial factors.
The fourth right abandonment takes as its object the arisen remedial factors. As stated in the Sūtra, this should be explained in detail through such correlations.
The essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) refers to the diligence (*vīrya*) that arises with respect to the four objects.

The accompaniments (*sahāya*) of the right abandonments refer to the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) associated with that diligence. The cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the right abandonments refers to what is taught in the Sūtra:
"Generating desire, exerting oneself, initiating right effort, uplifting the mind, and sustaining the mind. Herein, these phrases reveal the cultivation of right effort (*vīrya*) and its basis.

Cessation (*śamatha*). As for that which is the basis of cessation, it refers to desire (*chanda*), because one initiates diligence preceded by desire. Right effort (*samyakpradhāna*) refers to exertion and so forth.

Among the mental attentions (*manasikāra*) regarding the signs of cessation, arousal, and equanimity, when one attends to the signs of cessation and so forth, does not look back with longing at the objective sphere (*ālambana-viṣaya*), and purely cultivates the antidote, at that time it is called exertion (*vyāyāma*), intended for the purpose of diminishing laxity (*laya*).
He eliminates lethargy and initiates right effort. Why is this?
When the secondary affliction of lethargy arises, he trains his mind by means of mental orientations such as the pure and sublime in order to diminish it.
When secondary afflictions such as restlessness arise, he restrains and sustains his mind through the method of internal realization and withdrawal. At that time, it is called "initiating."

Right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*) is precisely the skillful means for manifesting this reduction of laxity (*laya*) and excitement (*auddhatya*); therefore, it is subsequently stated that one "exerts the mind" and "upholds the mind.
Furthermore, there is another meaning, as explained in the section on the gates of interpretation (*arthamukha*) mentioned previously. As for the fruit of cultivating right effort:

This means that one completely abandons all that is to be countered; regarding the antidotes, whether they are attained or realized, they should be understood as corresponding respectively [to the four right abandonments].
Thus, the five gateways of the right abandonments have been briefly explained.
Next, the five gates within the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) are explained. Regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*) of the bases of psychic power:

it refers to the phenomena upon which one dwells when meditative concentration (*samādhi*) has been fully perfected. Furthermore, what is this? It is the various miraculous transformations and such phenomena that are initiated by the power of perfected *samādhi*;
these constitute the objective sphere. Regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the bases of psychic power: it is *samādhi*. Regarding the aids to the bases of psychic power...
The "companions" refer to desire (*chanda*), diligence (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*), as well as the mental states and mental factors associated with them.

The "cultivation of the bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda-bhāvanā*) refers to the frequent cultivation of the eight types of formative acts of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*), namely: desire, diligence, faith, serenity, right mindfulness, right awareness, volition, and equanimity.
These eight types are briefly subsumed into four: application (*prayoga*), maintenance (*parigraha*), continuity (*anubandha*), and antidote (*pratipakṣa*). Regarding "application":
The practitioner consists of desire (*chanda*), diligence (*vīrya*), and faith (*śraddhā*). Desire is the basis for diligence, and faith is the cause of desire. Why is this so?
Because through the seeking of desire, one exerts diligent effort in order to attain this goal. Such seeking of desire does not exist apart from faithful acceptance.
Because they possess a substantial nature (*dravya*) and so forth. "Appropriation" refers to pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), for by means of this pliancy, one benefits and sustains both body and mind.

"Continuity" refers to right mindfulness (*smṛti*) and right situational awareness (*samprajanya*); because one does not forget the object of focus and settles the mind upon a single point, and because one knows reality as it is whenever negligence arises.
"Antidote" refers to volition (*cetanā*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*), which are the two applications (*prayoga*) of exerting the mind and sustaining the mind.

Power: because it can distance oneself from the already arisen states of lethargy and agitation; and because it can induce the characteristics of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and so forth, which remove latent afflictions (*anuśaya*).

Furthermore, there are two types of cultivation for desire, effort, mind, and investigation: namely, cultivation that combines the causes and conditions of gathering and dispersing, and cultivation of distancing.
It is neither deficient nor distracted; it is the cultivation that accords with the basis of those two.

Herein, desire and so forth are shown to be the causes and conditions for the two types of cultivation—namely, concentration and distraction. As for the cause and condition for concentration, it refers to being far removed from *vipaśyanā*.
The causes of sinking (*laya*) arising from laziness and of distraction (*vikṣepa*) are as follows: the former is due to being far removed from the sign of impurity (*aśubha-nimitta*);

the latter arises through the gateway of agitation (*auddhatya*), whereby there is inner restlessness. As for "the collection of elation" (*unnati-pakṣa*), it refers to [distraction] arising through the gateway of torpor and sleep (*styāna-middha*).

"Distraction" (*vikṣepa*) refers to wandering outwardly through the gateway of conforming to signs of purity and excellence (*śubha-praṇīta-nimitta*). "Not inferior and conforming to cultivation" (*an-hīna-anulomika-bhāvanā*) refers to...
Regarding the cultivation that accords with non-distraction through the observation of signs: this refers to observing phenomena such as hair and body hair by relying on the sign of impurity.
Regarding the cultivation that accords with the basis for those two: this refers to cultivating the basis of light.
Thus, in this sequence, the Blessed One said: "My desire and inclination are neither inferior nor arrogant. Regarding...
Not gathering within, nor dispersing without, one possesses the perception of before and after, as well as the perception of above and below.
One develops the mind, becomes free from entanglements, and dwells together with light, cultivating the mind for oneself: "May my mind be free from all darkness and obscuration.
Thus far, the Abhidharma treatise has been explained; herein, regarding the observation of characteristics, those who observe all phenomena reveal that.

The sūtra mentions "prior and posterior" and "above and below" to develop the mind. Regarding the observation of the hair and so forth based on the sign of impurity (*aśubha-nimitta*), this reveals that those sūtras and the notions of prior, posterior, above, and below serve to distance one from the fetters (*paryavasthāna*). What, then, are called "posterior and prior" and "above and below"?

As stated in the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "When practicing *śamatha*, one cultivates the perception of the upper and lower parts of the body within the category of mental application (*citta-pakṣa*).
When practicing *vipaśyanā*, one cultivates the perception of the front and back parts within the category of observation (*vipaśyanā-pakṣa*). Regarding the perception of the upper and lower parts:
this refers to observing this body exactly as it is situated and exactly as it is intended, from the crown of the head above down to the soles of the feet below."
It is filled with various kinds of impurities, namely all the various hairs, body hair, nails, and teeth within this body, as described extensively above.
Regarding the "perception of the preceding and following": it refers to a certain person who, with earnestness and sincerity, attends to the object of observation.

One skillfully grasps, skillfully reflects, skillfully understands, and skillfully penetrates; that is, while standing one observes sitting, while sitting one observes lying down, or while walking behind one observes those walking ahead.
Thus, when it is said that "while standing one observes sitting," this demonstrates observing future knowable formations by means of present mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Why is this? Because the stage of present mental attention has already [passed].

Because it has manifested in the present life, it is called "dwelling. Because that which is to be known in the future has not yet manifested in the present and is on the verge of arising, it is called "sitting.

Furthermore, when it is said that "sitting one observes lying down," this indicates observing past conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—the objects of knowledge—by means of present mental attention (*manasikāra*). Why is this so? Because the stage of present mental attention is on the verge of...
Because it is about to cease, it is called "sitting. Because the state of what was previously known has already passed away and ceased, it is called "lying down.

Furthermore, if it is said that "sometimes one walks behind while observing what is ahead," this demonstrates that by means of present mental attention (*manasikāra*), one observes the mental attention that has just ceased in the immediate past. Why is this so? Because it has already arisen, [it is] immediately...

That which has just ceased is called the "preceding" attention (*manasikāra*) that is the object of apprehension. If, immediately following this, a newly arisen "apprehending" attention takes up that which has just ceased in the preceding moment, it is called the "succeeding" [attention].
One should know that herein, for the sake of cultivating calm (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*), [these two are established].

One cultivates the two types of superior perception of light; this is called cultivation through perception (*saṃjñā-bhāvanā*). The remaining phrases should be understood by analogy according to their mutual connection.
This is called the characteristic of the cultivation of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). As for the fruit of cultivating the bases of psychic power:

because one has already thoroughly cultivated and refined meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is able to penetrate and manifest whatever dharmas one wishes to realize, in accordance with one's mind. Furthermore, regarding...
Within each respective sphere of phenomena, one attains mastery and the capacity for sovereign action;

according to one's aspirations and inclinations, one can accomplish various feats such as supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and further induce superior qualities. Such is the brief explanation of the five doors of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Next, the distinctions of the five faculties are explained through five gates. Regarding the objects of the five faculties: if categorized by their common operation, they take the four noble truths as their object;
if categorized by their uncommon operation, they take the non-analytical truths (apratiṣṭhita-satya) as their object. Regarding the intrinsic nature of the five faculties:
these are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. Regarding the companions of the five faculties: these are the mental states and mental factors associated with them. Five...

Regarding the cultivation of the faculties (*indriya*): it means that through the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), one cultivates the practice of patience (*kṣānti*) toward the truths; through the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*), one cultivates the practice of vigor for the sake of awakening;

through the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), one cultivates the practice of non-forgetfulness; through the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), one cultivates the practice of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*);
and through the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), one cultivates the practice of discernment (*pravicaya*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The faculty of faith is faith in the One..."
All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; they are inverted and false perceptions, existing neither in the past, nor in the future, nor in the present.
One believes that all phenomena are empty, signless, and without volitional action, neither arising nor ceasing;

yet one also believes in and upholds the dharmas of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, even up to the faculty of wisdom—regarding these as the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
It functions harmoniously without obstruction or difficulty; it is without sorrow regarding the world and without elation regarding nirvāṇa.
Because one attains sovereign wisdom, it is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). This is a brief description of the cultivation of the five faculties.

As for the fruit of cultivating the five faculties, it means that one is able to swiftly give rise to the direct realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*); by the power of this predominance, one will before long be able to produce the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Furthermore...

Having cultivated *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*, and having induced *kṣānti* and the *laukikāgradharma*, one immediately manifests this body and enters the stage of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Thus, the five faculties and the five gates are briefly explained.
Next, the five powers (*pañcabala*) are explained through five gates of differentiation. The first four gates are similar to those of the faculties (*indriya*);

they differ only slightly in that they are the fruit of cultivation. That is to say, they are able to diminish hindrances such as lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), cannot be overcome, and are superior to the former.
The five powers are briefly explained in this way through these five gates.
Next, the characteristics of the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are explained through five gates. Regarding the object of focus (*ālambana*) of the factors of enlightenment:

if one follows the gate of the established truths (*vyavasthāna-satya*) of the two vehicles, it is the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) as revealed therein; if one follows the gate of the established and non-established truths (*vyavasthāna-avyavasthāna-satya*) of the bodhisattvas, it takes the emptiness of both persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) as its objective sphere.

Regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the factors of enlightenment: it consists of mindfulness (*smṛti*), investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), diligence (*vīrya*), joy (*prīti*), and tranquility (*praśrabdhi*).

Equanimity. Thus, these seven factors constitute the essence of the limbs of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*). Furthermore, these seven factors are subsumed under three categories, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*:

three limbs of awakening are subsumed under the category of calm abiding (*śamatha*), one limb of awakening is subsumed under the category of insight (*vipaśyanā*), and one is subsumed under both categories.
Therefore, they are called the seven limbs of awakening; namely: investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), diligence (*vīrya*), and joy (*prīti*).
These three are subsumed under the category of *vipaśyanā* (insight). Concentration (*samādhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are subsumed under the category of *śamatha* (calm abiding).

The single factor of the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is subsumed under both categories; this is designated as the "range of activity" (*gocara*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The awakening factor of mindfulness exists in two places:
it can gather wholesome dharmas and can ward off unwholesome dharmas, like a gatekeeper who allows those who are beneficial to enter and excludes those who are not."
When the mind sinks, one brings to mind the three factors for its arousal; when it is distracted, one brings to mind the three factors for its withdrawal.

As for the attendants of the awakening factors (*bodhyaṅga*), these refer to the associated mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitta*). Regarding the cultivation of the awakening factors, there are both common and uncommon types.
The characteristics of their common cultivation are as explained in the Abhidharma: they depend upon seclusion, dispassion, cessation, and are dedicated toward relinquishment.

One cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, up to the awakening factor of equanimity. These four phrases, in their respective order, demonstrate the cultivation of the awakening factors by taking the Truths as objects.

Why is this? When one takes the Truth of Suffering as an object and experiences it as suffering, because one seeks seclusion from that objective realm of suffering, it is called "relying on seclusion.
When one takes the aspect of craving as the origin of suffering and takes it as an object...
Regarding the object (*ālambana*): because one necessarily seeks the departure from desire (*vairāgya*), it is called "relying on the departure from desire.

If one takes the cessation of suffering (*nirodha*) as the object, at the time of that cessation of suffering, because one necessarily seeks its realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) regarding this object, it is called "relying [on cessation]. Regarding "peaceful abandonment" (*śāntaprahāṇa*):

this refers to the practice of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; by the power of this, because one abandons suffering and necessarily seeks to cultivate [this state] regarding this object, it is so named.
Dedicating and relinquishing [merit] is called common cultivation. As for uncommon cultivation, it is as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
not recollecting and not being mindful of any phenomena is called the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Seeking within all phenomena for wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate phenomena, and finding that none of them can be apprehended, is called the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Not entering the three realms and destroying all...

The characteristic of the elements (*dhātu*) is called the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Because it does not give rise to attachment or pleasure toward any conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), and because the characteristics of sorrow and joy increase [therein], it is called the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Because one cannot find any mental object (*ālambana*) among all phenomena, it is called the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
That all phenomena possess the characteristic of constant concentration—neither distracted nor non-concentrated—is called the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Regarding...
Not being attached to nor relying upon any phenomena, and not even perceiving this mind of equanimity—this is called the factor of awakening of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Furthermore, when joy arises from the wisdom that contemplates the true nature of reality, this is called true joy. Having attained this true joy, one first eliminates physical joy.
Next, one eliminates mental joy. Thereafter, by eliminating all marks of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), one attains bliss that pervades the body and the mind;

this is the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-sambodhyaṅga*). Having attained joy, one abandons all contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), namely: the contemplations of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness;

and the contemplations of existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, and so forth. Why is this? Because the absence of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). If one does not practice equanimity...
Thereupon, various disputes arise. If one takes "existence" to be real and "non-existence" to be false, and if one takes "non-existence" to be real, then one takes "existence" to be false;
if one takes "neither existence nor non-existence" to be real, then one takes "existence and non-existence" to be false.

One becomes attached to what is deemed real and feels aversion toward what is deemed false, giving rise to places of sorrow and joy. How can one not abandon this? Having attained such joy, one eliminates and abandons the seven [types of craving].

The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) are fully perfected. Within this context, "removal" (*praśrabdhi*) refers to that which eliminates heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*); thus it is called "removal.

This is a brief explanation of the characteristics of the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment. As for the fruit of cultivating the branches of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), it consists of the permanent abandonment of those afflictions to be severed through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, as for the specific fruit of the factors of enlightenment, it is being born into the family of the Buddhas and being free from the five fears.

One attains the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas, shakes a hundred Buddha-worlds, and so forth; these are explained at length as in the sūtras. The five gates of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) have been briefly explained in this way.

Next, the five gates of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) are clarified. As for the object of focus (*ālambana*) of the eightfold noble path, it refers to that very same [object] at a subsequent time.

The suchness of the Four Noble Truths, as well as the entirety of all things in their "exhaustive nature" (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and "suchness" (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*), are all objects of focus during the stage of the path of cultivation.
