As for the essence of the Eightfold Noble Path, it consists of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; one should know that these eight factors constitute the body of the limbs of the path. Furthermore—

These eight factors are subsumed within three aggregates, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*. Among these, right view, right thought, and right effort are subsumed within the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*);

right speech, right action, and right livelihood are subsumed within the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*); and right mindfulness and right concentration are subsumed within the aggregate of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*).
Why, then, are the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) subsumed under three categories, while these factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are said to be subsumed under three aggregates?

This is to demonstrate that on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are practiced in union, whereas on other paths of skillful means they cannot be so combined.

It is also to demonstrate the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), wherein by cultivating these three aggregates, one attains the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktiskandha*) and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanaskandha*) belonging to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The companions of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) refer to the mental states and mental factors associated with them. Regarding the cultivation of the factors of the path:

as for those that function in common [with other factors], it is as explained in the context of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); as for those that do not function in common, it is as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The Bodhisattva, regarding all phenomena as empty and unapprehendable, abides within such right view and contemplates the characteristics of right thought, knowing the nature of all volitions.
All such thoughts are indeed erroneous, even those contemplating nirvāṇa or contemplating the Buddhas; one knows them all to be so. Why is this?
Because the severing of all conceptualization and discrimination is called right thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*). Abiding within such right thought—
Not seeing this as either right or wrong, transcending all conceptualization and discrimination—this is right intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
All conceptualization and discrimination are entirely equal; because they are equal, the mind does not cling. Such as these are called right intention.
This is explained at length, up to: "The fruit of cultivating the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) is the manifestation of the ocean of discrimination to others, causing them to have faith."
It purifies afflictions, it purifies secondary afflictions, and it purifies the obstacles to supreme qualities, because it enables the attainment of immeasurable and preeminent qualities.
This is a brief explanation of the five gates of the path factors (*mārgāṅga*). Such is the summary exposition of the meaning of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).

Next, I shall explain the text. Within the text, the exposition of the treatise is first initiated. This consists of two phrases: the first phrase provides a general initiation, while the subsequent phrase initiates the specific [discussion].
Regarding the "first statement" in this treatise, it refers to the teaching on the four foundations of mindfulness at the beginning of this chapter.
The verses in this section comprise twelve and a half stanzas in total. Within them, there are two parts:

the first eleven stanzas specifically explain the remedies (*pratipakṣa*), while the final one and a half stanzas provide a general summary of the remedies. Regarding the first eleven stanzas, there are six sections:

first, the initial stanza clarifies the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); second, the following stanza clarifies the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*); third, three and a half stanzas clarify the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

The four [sections] comprise two verses that generally clarify the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*). The fifth section consists of one and a half verses clarifying the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*). The sixth section consists of two verses clarifying the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Within the first verse, the upper half specifically reveals [the first factor], while the lower half provides a general clarification. Thus, the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are established.
There are briefly three intentions [for establishing the foundations of mindfulness]: first, to counteract the four inversions; second, to liberate from the four bonds;
and third, to enter the Four Noble Truths. The distinctions among these three types have already been explained previously. Now, within this context, the third meaning is discussed.

Regarding the statement "coarse practice," this refers to the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). All physical bodies are accompanied by heaviness and rigidity (*dausthulya*) and are devoid of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*). This is...

The characteristic of suffering in conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Therefore, one contemplates the body as entering into the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). Regarding the phrase "the cause of craving," this reveals the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).

From various kinds of feelings, the six types of craving arise; craving gathers together the mass of suffering within the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*). This is why one contemplates this [feeling], for it enables entry into the Truth of Suffering.
Regarding the phrase "the seeds," this reveals the foundation of mindfulness of mind (*citta-smṛtyupasthāna*). The mind holds the seeds and acts as the root of all phenomena. I am...

□□. Because one observes the mind as it truly is and enters the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), there is fear of annihilation. Regarding "not being deluded": this reveals the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Because ignorance fails to comprehend the various categories of phenomena and their distinctions between defilement and purity, it obscures clear wisdom;

thus, by not being deluded regarding the characteristics of phenomena, one accords with and enters the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). In the second half [of the verse], the phrase "for the sake of entering the four truths" reveals the general [purpose].

Regarding the practice of cultivating the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catur-smṛtyupasthāna*), this generally clarifies the capacity for cultivation. The commentary consists of two parts:

first, the explanation of the first half [of the verse]; second, the explanation of the second half. Within the first part, specifically regarding the explanation of "gross activities" (*audārika-carita*), there is first a brief explanation of the text, followed by a detailed analysis.
Regarding the initial statement that "coarse activity (*audārika-carita*) becomes manifest by means of the body," this is as explained in the *Abhidharma*:

all physical bodies possess the characteristic of suffering-as-activity (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), because they are manifested by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*). Therefore, when practicing meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) that serves as the antidote to this [suffering] arises with differentiation within the body.
What is now referred to as "coarse activity becoming manifest" refers to the manifestation of the suffering-as-activity consisting of coarse heaviness. This...

The section beginning with "the body" and below further clarifies the preceding meaning. Regarding the statement that "that which is coarse and great is the characteristic of the suffering of conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*): the term "great" signifies "heavy.

This means that "coarse-heaviness" (*dausthulya*) is the characteristic of the suffering of conditioned existence. The remainder of the text is self-evident. Therefore, the following section provides a general explanation of the second half [of the verse].
Next, one cultivates right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*). First, this initiates the following section. Herein, secondly, the four right efforts are explained. There are two parts to the verse:
the first half excels the preceding by initiating what follows; the second half connects with the preceding to manifest right effort.

As previously stated in the context of the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*), one has already known that defiled phenomena are not aids to the path, and one also knows that pure phenomena are [aids].
Because they are the antidotes to those [defilements], it is said that "having known" and so forth, up to "the antidote.

Just as with the aforementioned defiled phenomena—those already arisen are extinguished and those not yet arisen do not arise—for the sake of the superior pure phenomena, those not yet arisen are caused to arise and those already arisen are increased.

Therefore, it is said that one cultivates the four right efforts for the sake of these two superior goals. In the commentary there are two parts; first, the explanation of the first half [of the verse] is for the purpose of abandoning and extinguishing.
Below. Next, the latter half [of the verse] is explained; its textual structure is clear.

This section on the three supernormal knowledges (*vidyā*) and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) consists of three and a half verses, which are divided into three sections. The first line sets forth their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
The second line explains the name [of the practice]. The final three verses clarify the characteristics of cultivation. Regarding the initial statement, "abiding therein according with the task":

having previously cultivated right effort to eliminate evil and produce good, one abides in one-pointedness of mind (ekāgratā) by following those tasks that are free from hindrances and possess assistance.
The objects of the mind’s focus do not exceed two types: namely, coarse and distracted objects, and objects of meditative concentration (dhyāna).
Having abandoned these scattered and coarse objects, one dwells in those meditative absorption (dhyāna) objects; for this reason, it is said that "one dwells therein.
This clarifies that the mind abides in one-pointedness (ekāgratā), which is the essential nature of the four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda).

Because concentration is attained by following the four types of predominance (adhipati), it is next stated that they serve to "accomplish what has been taught"; this is the second explanation of the meaning of accomplishing the bases of psychic power.
"Yathā-kāma" (as one wishes) means "according to intention. "Pāda" (foot/limb) means "that which fulfills. Whatever one desires is accomplished without exception;

this is the meaning of mastery over the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*). These six supernormal powers are called "the bases of power" (*ṛddhi-pāda*) because they are like feet that must be used to reach a destination.

Just as one must have two feet to go anywhere, the term "pāda" is explained here by what is required [to achieve the goal]. Taking the fruit as the name for the cause, they are called "bases of power" (*ṛddhi-pāda*). This...
The final three verses clarify the characteristics of cultivation. This section contains two parts: first, the initial two lines present the number and provide a general indication;

second, the subsequent two and a half verses provide a detailed explanation according to their sequence. Within the general indication, there are also two parts: the first line indicates the practice to be cultivated and what is to be abandoned;
the second line indicates that which is to be attained.
The commentary consists of two parts: first, the explanation of the first half [of the verse]; second, the explanation of the latter half. Within the first part, there are also two sections:
the specific explanation and the general clarification. In the specific explanation, the first phrase is explained first. This also has two parts: the direct explanation and the further elucidation.

Regarding the direct explanation, the statement "having already applied right effort to abandon... cites the object to be pursued in order to explain the word "matter" (*vastu*). Next, the word "mind" (*citta*) is mentioned.

The phrase "there is no manifesting of existence" refers to the auxiliary factor that follows the mind. Next, the character *sui* (following) is explained; thus, the phrase "attaining stability" explains abiding therein.

The section beginning with "this mind" below reiterates the preceding meaning. The statement "this mind’s abiding has four capacities" means that this mental abiding possesses four superior capacities, namely:
aspiration (*chanda*), exertion (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*). These four capacities function as follows... [but] only.

The mind abides through the accomplishment of each task, and by following the instructions of the spiritual teacher for each one, one attains the accomplishment of one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*).
Therefore, it is said that "one attains accomplishment by following the teachings. As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 98:

If there is a bhikṣu who, relying on pure intention and intense aspiration, desiring to realize the most excellent supernormal knowledge, listens to the true Dharma with profound reverence and respect from the Tathāgatas and their disciples; immediately upon hearing it, [he applies himself].
One gradually realizes a superior samādhi; this is called the samādhi predominant in desire (*chanda-adhipateya-samādhi*).

Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, regarding the Dharma as he has heard it and the Dharma as he has attained it, exerts great effort and arouses great diligence—either by correctly proclaiming and explaining it to others, or by reciting it with sublime intention and words—and from that point on, through immediate succession and gradual causes and conditions...
Being able to successively attain superior samādhi is called "samādhi predominant in diligence.
Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who properly grasps and contemplates the characteristics of various virtuous samādhis, observing the stages from the livid corpse up to the skeletal chain as the limit.
Through this object of focus, he successively gives rise to superior samādhi; this is called "samādhi predominant in mind."

The Higher Samādhi. Furthermore, there is a bhikṣu who, regarding the Dharma as he has heard it and the Dharma as he has attained it, dwells alone in a secluded place, reflecting upon it, deliberating upon it, and examining it with thorough discernment.
By means of these causes and conditions, he gradually gives rise to superior samādhi.

This is called the "samādhi of superior observation," and so forth, as explained at length. Thus, these four types of persons all achieve supreme concentration (samādhi) in accordance with the teachings they have heard;
therefore, it is said that they attain accomplishment by following the instructions. From this point downward, the second phrase is explained.

Within this, there are two parts. First, regarding the statement that "attaining accomplishment by following the instructions" is what is called the "four bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*), this raises the general category to clarify the name before proceeding to explain its meaning.
From "all" onwards is the formal explanation of the name itself.

The phrase "the accomplishment of all sought-after aims" is the formal explanation of the term "for the sake of accomplishment" (*siddhaye*) within the verse. The mention of "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) is the explanation of what is required.

Regarding the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) in the passage below: because it is the causal factor for the dharma through which all sought-after objectives are accomplished according to one's wish, this meditative concentration is called the "basis of psychic power" (*ṛddhipāda*).
The separate explanation of the two phrases was completed previously; here, the following portion generally clarifies their meaning.
Within that, the first phrase reiterates the essential nature of the basis of psychic power, while the subsequent phrase provides a concluding clarification, stated in sequential order.

Regarding the initial statement that "the mind abiding" is called *samādhi*—which here is translated as "equipoise"—in order to clarify what is meant by the mind abiding, one takes only the ninth stage among the nine types of abiding, namely equipoise (*samāhita*), as the essence of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).
What are the names of these nine types of mental abiding? First, internal abiding; second, even abiding; third, settled abiding; fourth...
1. Abiding nearby; 2. pliancy; 3. adaptability; 4. fitness; 5. submissiveness; 6. tranquility; 7. supreme tranquility; 8. one-pointedness of focus; 9. meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Because of the causes and conditions of repeated cultivation, repeated practice, and frequent intensive cultivation, one attains a state that is effortless and spontaneous, a path that proceeds naturally;
therefore, it is called meditative concentration. Meditative concentration is precisely *samādhi*.

This is the ground (*bhūmi*). The first eight types of abiding will be explained further below. Regarding the phrase "should be known," it is an exhortation to understand the meaning of such meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Therefore, the second section concludes by clarifying that because one has diligently practiced according to the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*) within the stages of the first eight mental abidings, one subsequently attains the ninth abiding in *samādhi*. Thus, it is spoken of as follows after the right efforts.

This refers to the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Following the preceding section, the latter half [of the verse] is now explained. Regarding the phrase "dwelling according to the matter and according to the teaching":

this restates the previously mentioned essence of the bases of psychic power. By relying on internal diligent application and external sacred teachings, one attains the stability of mind through these causes and conditions;
hence, it is said that one "dwells according to the matter and according to the teaching. The internal and external causes and conditions have already been explained as before. Because...
By what skillful means is this dwelling accomplished? It is by extinguishing the five faults and cultivating the eight practices as their supporting roots that one attains mental abiding;
therefore it is said, "for the purpose of extinguishing... and so forth, up to "should be known. This intent clarifies the time when the four dhyānas are attained.
One must possess these eight kinds of requisites to achieve that samādhi. According to the Abhidharma treatises (*Abhidharmapiṭaka*), it should be explained in this way;
however, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, there is another interpretation. Regarding the cultivation of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), there are two levels.
First, by relying on the predominant power of the four factors—desire and so forth—one attains samādhi as appropriate; this is merely the cessation [of obstacles].

While the active fetters (*paryavasthāna*) are manifest and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have not yet been abandoned, that person later desires to abandon those latent tendencies and further cultivates the eight modes of exertion (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*).

Thereby, they achieve the most excellent meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Taken together, these two stages—prior and subsequent—are established as the essential nature of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Therefore, the phrase "dwelling according to the matter and according to the instruction" now refers back to what was stated previously.

Regarding the stage: for the four persons who have attained meditative concentration and below, it is clarified that these four persons subsequently cultivate eight kinds of formative acts of abandonment (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*) as appropriate to their respective cases.
Generally speaking, these eight kinds of practices also exist in the preceding stage;

however, because in that stage one merely suppresses the manifest entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), the designation "formative acts of abandonment" is not established there. It is only in the subsequent stage that one is able to abandon the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Drowsiness. Therefore, it is here that the "abandoning applications" (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) are established. As that treatise states:
"By the predominant power of the four *samādhis*, one has already distanced oneself from the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*);

subsequently, for the sake of permanently destroying the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and for the sake of cultivating those wholesome dharmas that serve as their antidotes, one further gives rise to desire, zeal, and exertion. Thus, he correctly practices in this manner.

At that time, there are eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*) which function in a differentiated manner for the sake of permanently destroying all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and for the sake of attaining the perfection of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Among these, "desire" (*chanda*) is itself that desire; "exertion" (*vyāyāma*) is itself that diligence (*vīrya*);
"faith" (*śraddhā*) is itself that faith; and "established mindfulness," "clear comprehension," "volition," and "equanimity" are themselves those skillful means (*upāya*).
Thus, herein, when the four *samādhis*— beginning with desire (*chanda*)— and the eight kinds of exertions (*prahāṇa-saṃskāra*) now described,

are fully accomplished for the sake of permanently severing all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are collectively termed the "basis of psychic power consisting of the accomplishment of the exertion of *samādhi* through desire," and so on,
up to the "basis of psychic power consisting of the accomplishment of the exertion of *samādhi* through investigation."
The bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*). [This continues] up to the detailed explanation. As for the statement "desire here," that refers to the desire for that;
up to "that very means" (*upāya*), this clarifies that when those four persons previously cultivated the four dhyānas, they likewise possessed these eight modes of activity (*ākāra*).
For when those four persons practiced meditative concentration, there was none who attained it without relying upon this desire, diligence, faith, and means.

Regarding "concentration" (*samādhi*): at that time, they are collectively referred to as four. In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, they are not termed the "eight applications for abandonment" (*aṣṭau prahāṇasaṃskārāḥ*).
Although the specific name "applications for abandonment" is not established there, their functional characteristics (*ākāra*) do not differ from those here;

therefore, it is said that these are indeed those. Furthermore, although all four persons possess desire and so forth, the four distinctions are taught according to what is predominant in each, and not because...

Regarding those for whom desire is predominant, there is no practice of diligence and so forth; likewise, up to those for whom contemplation is predominant, there is no practice of desire and so forth.
Let us now set aside the discussion of the vehicles and return to explaining the main text. What follows below serves as the introduction to the subsequent passage. From this point onward:
There are two and a half verses. Based on the previous general heading, they are now explained in detail in successive order.

Specifically, the first verse clarifies the five kinds of faults, while the subsequent one and a half verses clarify the eight formative forces of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*). Within the former, there are two parts: three lines that explain them individually and one line that summarizes them collectively.
The characteristics of these five losses are clearly explained in the commentary. In the commentary, the five kinds of losses are explained in sequence.
Regarding the first, "sinking into a state of indolence and evil" means being attached to a state of distraction and failing to arouse diligence.

Regarding the second, "not recollecting and not upholding" means not recollecting the words of the teaching and not upholding the purport of the teaching. Regarding the third, "having sorrow and joy as its essence" means...

Laxity is sorrow; it is sorrowful regarding the difficulty of progress, and its functional activity is sinking. Excitement is joy; it rejoices in minor attainments, and its functional activity is agitation.

These two depend upon one another and mutually pervade as obstacles; therefore, they are established together as a single fault, just as the combination of annihilationism and eternalism is considered a single extreme view.
The fourth fault is: practicing insight during a state of sinking, and [practicing calm] during a state of agitation...
One cultivates *śamatha*, yet does not cultivate it through timely mental attention (*manasikāra*). Therefore, failing to apply mental attention constitutes a fault. The fifth fault is as follows:

when sinking and excitation have subsided, one should simply remain in equanimity. If, after sinking has subsided, one still applies the intention of "leaving" (*vairāgya*), then sinking will arise again.

If, after excitation has ceased, one still applies the intention of "stopping" (*sthiti*), one will likewise fall back into sinking. Therefore, one should not apply mental attention at these two [specific] times.

This serves as an introduction. The section beginning with "To eliminate" below clarifies the practice of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*). This also first initiates the discourse; within it, there are three sentences.

The first sentence provides a general heading by establishing eight kinds of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The second sentence specifically elucidates the establishment of the first four intentions. Furthermore, the section beginning with "To eliminate" below formally introduces the subsequent text.
There are two parts in this verse. The first two lines clarify the preceding four practices; the subsequent one verse reveals the latter four practices.
The first four practices collectively counteract a single hindrance. The reason for this is that among all hindrances, laziness is the foremost.
To dispel these difficulties, one must rely on the mutual dependence of the desire and diligence as the basis and the object, along with the assistance of faith and pliancy as cause and effect.
By relying on these four powers, one is then able to subdue the latter four faults; having lost their leadership, the power of these hindrances becomes weak and inferior.

Each one can remove [the respective obstacle]. Regarding the "basis" (*āśraya*): this refers to the first, which is desire (*chanda*). As for the "dependent" (*āśrita*): this refers to the second, right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*).
This is because, having first developed a profound aspiration for the qualities of tranquility, one initiates diligent exertion based upon that. These are the causal conditions.
The cause of the basis is the third faith, because it gives rise to the desire for certainty. Regarding "speech and fruit," these are the fruits of that which depends [upon them];
this is the fourth, serenity (*praśrabdhi*), because one attains the fruit of serenity by taking right effort as its cause.

Regarding the sequence in the explanation: this explains these four types. As for the statement in the fourth [category], "If one applies right effort, one attains the meditative concentration (dhyāna) sought," at the time of attaining meditative concentration, the heavy and coarse states (dausthulya) are extinguished; therein, one immediately attains physical and mental pliancy (praśrabdhi).

Pliancy is termed *praśrabdhi*; its characteristic is that of being agreeable and refreshing. Therefore, by way of attaining concentration, the fruit of pliancy is manifested. The remaining four [categories] below clarify the subsequent stages.

Regarding the four practices, they are likewise first initiated. Within this, the number is first stated and the names are enumerated; from "extinguishing the remainder" onwards, they are explained in contrast to the faults.

Next, the four lines of the verse manifest the four characteristics in succession. The first line, "not being deluded regarding the objective sphere," refers to right mindfulness as the antidote to forgetting the teachings.
The next line, "being able to discern the high and the low," refers to right knowledge as the antidote to the third [fault].

Transgression. To be aware of sinking and floating—floating being high and sinking being low—is to be aware as these states arise. "To extinguish the mental effort (*citta-karman*) of that" refers to the application of attention (*manasikāra*).
This means applying the mind with attention in order to extinguish sinking and floating, giving rise to the appropriate antidote as needed. This is the application of attention within this context.

This is precisely the mental factor of *manasikāra* (attention). It is called *manasikāra* because it initiates and impels *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; it is not the *manasikāra* that is included among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).

Regarding "releasing during the state of tranquility": this clarifies the characteristic of equanimity (*upekṣā*), which is to relinquish by allowing [the mind] to settle naturally once sinking and excitement have been extinguished.

In the commentary, there are four points. Regarding the fourth point, the statement "arousing a mind of relinquishment and allowing it to flow in a continuous stream" is intended to clarify that the stage of equanimity (*upekṣā*) has a beginning, middle, and end.
As stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*: "Equanimity is based upon right effort and is free from greed, hatred, and delusion."

It is the opposite of abiding in affliction (*saṃkleśa*). Its essence consists of the mind’s equanimity (*samatā*), the mind’s rectitude (*rjutā*), and the mind’s state of effortless abiding (*anābhoga-vihāritā*).
Its function is to serve as a basis that does not admit afflictions. Regarding "the mind’s equanimity" and so forth:

this distinguishes the specific types of equanimity (*upekṣā*) according to the initial, middle, and final stages. Why is this? Because equanimity is associated with the mind and is free from sinking (*laya*) and other such states.
Because of the state of inequality, one first realizes the mind’s state of equanimity (*citta-samatā*).

Through the mind’s equanimity, one becomes free from applied effort (*prāyoga*) because it proceeds spontaneously and continuously. Subsequently, one realizes the mind’s state of rectitude (*citta-ṛjutā*). Through the mind’s rectitude, there is no [distraction] regarding the various defilements (*saṃkleśa*).
Finally, one realizes the mind’s state of dwelling without effort (*anābhoga-vihāra*). This is what is meant here by "arousing equanimity" (*upekṣā*).
"Mind" (*citta*) is the general heading. Next, the word "emission" (*visarga*) reveals the equality of mind in the first stage, because one initially emits and relinquishes inequality.
Next, the word "flow" (*pravāha*) reveals the rectitude of mind in the second stage, because from that equality flow the four types of rectitude.
The term "continuity" (*prabandha*) reveals the third stage, which is dwelling without effort (*anābhoga*), because it is free from...
Because their functional efficacy is maintained for a long duration.

Following the four bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*), this is the fourth major section, which generally elucidates the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*). These too are first brought forth; the textual structure is clear.

Within the verse, there are two parts. The first one and a half verses correctly clarify the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); the final two lines pertain to the respective stages (*avasthā*). Within the first part, there are three sections:
one verse clarifies the faculties (*indriya*), one line clarifies the powers (*bala*), and the final line clarifies the sequence of the five [faculties].

Within the first of these, there are also two sections: the preceding line reveals the cause for the arising of the faculties, while the following three lines correctly clarify the faculties themselves.

Regarding the characteristics: the phrase "having already descended" and so forth refers to the seeds of liberation (*mokṣa-bīja*). Since the stage of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) is situated within the stage of penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*), they have already previously descended from the seeds of liberation.
In relation to the fruit of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa-phala*), the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) thus cultivated serve as the initial seeds for the fruit of liberation;
therefore, it is said that they have "already descended" as seeds of liberation. As for which wholesome dharmas constitute their essence, some masters state:

It is said: Among the seven stages of expedient means (*saptaprayoga*), the first three expedient means constitute the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*). Since the four states of mind beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) constitute the stage conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), it is known that the first three belong to the stage conducive to liberation.

Some teachers further state that the two types of wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*), as well as the three karmas of giving, morality, and [patience], constitute the stage conducive to liberation.
As stated in the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*: "The essence of the stage conducive to liberation is..."

This refers to the actions of body, speech, and mind, which are attained through skillful means (*upāya*). There are two types of such means: first, hearing with the ear; second, reflection. Furthermore, there are three kinds: first, generosity (*dāna*);
second, ethical discipline (*śīla*); and third, extensive learning (*bahuśruta*). This is also stated accordingly in the *Vibhāṣā*.

Regarding these actions of body, speech, and mind, mental action (*manas-karman*) predominates. It belongs exclusively to the mental level (*manobhūmi*) and does not extend to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). This is the method.

It is indeed attained; it is also attained by birth. It is the wisdom resulting from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*), not the wisdom resulting from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).

By what means does one plant such roots of goodness? Whether through generosity, ethical discipline, or extensive learning, one dedicates these toward liberation and nirvāṇa, so as to forever leave behind saṃsāra.
If one possesses such a courageous mind, then one is able to plant them; if not, even if one [practices] much...
It is said in the treatises that even if one practices giving, maintains the precepts for a lifetime, and extensively cultivates great learning, one still cannot plant [the seeds of liberation].

If it is argued that the first three skillful means constitute the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), then since the establishment of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) encompasses all three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), why is it stated that they do not constitute "wisdom through cultivation" (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*)?
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The wholesome factors conducive to liberation are of two kinds: distant and proximate. As for the proximate..."
This refers to the seeds planted in previous bodies resulting in the accomplishment of this present body and liberation in a future body.

As for those who are distant, they have planted seeds over many *nayutas* of lifetimes and are unable to give rise to the "distant-part" wholesome roots (*dūrabhāgīya-kuśala*). The *Upāsaka-sūtra* explains it in the same way.
However, those śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of sharp faculties all cultivate the seven expedient means within their final body before parinirvāṇa, thereby attaining liberation.

If one detaches [the mind] and contemplates the general and specific foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), these are the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
One plants the seed for liberation within a single lifetime; how then can it be said that one must pass through three bodies?

Therefore, we know that the aforementioned roots of goodness of the preliminary expedients (*pūrvaprayoga*) belong to the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and are subsumed under the category of expedients. This is like the statement regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*): because it is an expedient for the link of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*), it belongs to consciousness.

[The same applies to] the branches (*aṅga*). Others say that generosity, ethical discipline, extensive learning, and the two types of skillful means are all the substance of the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).

However, these roots of goodness conducive to liberation consist of three grades. The middle and lower grades have hearing and reflection (*śruta-cintā*) as their substance; they possess the possibility of regression.
As for the superior grade, it has meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) as its substance; it serves as the vehicle for entering the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and is irreversible.

Regarding the meaning of "possibility of retrogression": the preceding explanation of the sūtras and śāstras concerns, for the time being, the first type [of roots], which reveals only the two inferior grades—the middling and lower—of the wholesome roots.

As the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya states: "From the lower and middling grades of the *mokṣabhāgīya* wholesome roots, there is the possibility of retrogression; this retrogression pertains only to their active manifestation (*samudācāra*)."

This is because it is not a habituation that can regress. Furthermore, in this treatise, the seeds of the lower stage of liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) are explained by way of the four right efforts and the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Therefore, one should know that these stages also pertain to the gateway of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmaya-prajñā*).

If these roots of goodness also pertain to cultivated wisdom, why are two distinct divisions with different characteristics established? The answer is: when faith (*śraddhā*) is predominant, the stage of liberation is established; when wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant, [the stage of penetration is established].
The stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) is established based on predominance (*adhipati*). As the Abhidharma treatise states:

"Regarding the dharmas that predominate with respect to the truths, the characteristic of pure faith and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) is the stage conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); regarding these very same dharmas, the characteristic of the patient acceptance of the investigation of dharmas (*dharmavicaya-kṣānti*) is the stage conducive to penetration.
Thus, in their respective order, there is predominance of faith and predominance of wisdom. Let us now conclude this digression and return to the explanation of the main text.

The following three phrases specifically clarify the five faculties (*pañcendriya*). "Supremacy of desire" is the characteristic of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), because if faith is predominant, there will necessarily be a longing for the object.
"Supremacy of activity" is the characteristic of the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*), because it possesses the capacity to perform the activity of abandoning evil and generating good.

"Non-confusion regarding the objective sphere" is the characteristic of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), because when mindfulness is predominant, one does not lose track of or become deluded about the object. Thus it is said.

That which is non-distracted is the characteristic of the faculty of concentration (*samādhi-indriya*). Furthermore, that which performs analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyāna*) is the characteristic of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñā-indriya*).

There are three parts to this explanation: first, the explanation of the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*); second, the explanation of the first phrase; and third, the explanation of the subsequent three phrases.
Regarding the initial statement, "herein [there is] predominance," the term "predominance" (*adhipati*) in the second phrase applies throughout all five locations.

Regarding the five bases (*pañca-sthāna*): because they possess the sense of "predominance" (*ādhipatya*), they carry the meaning of "faculties" (*indriya*). To cultivate these, the first phrase is explained as follows:

"For the sake of cultivating the four right efforts" (*catur-samyak-prahāṇa*) refers to the mention of the right efforts, while also including the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*). "The mind, having followed the teaching, has attained stability" refers to the citation of the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhi-pādāḥ*).
"The mind’s faith in this cause [of liberation]—from this point on, it is the seeds of the factors conducive to liberation" (*mokṣa-bhāgīya-bīja*) is... [the remainder].

It is known from this text that the third and fourth [stages] constitute the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*). Thus, these three and four stages precede the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*).
First, the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*) below the stage of desire are explained individually; the text is clear and can be understood accordingly.
The first line of the verse clarifies the second point, the exposition of power (*bala*). Specifically, regarding the exposition of power in terms of the five dharmas:

because one is able to diminish the afflictions (*kleśa*) at the time of superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*), it is said that "power is taught" due to the diminishing of afflictions. The subsequent line clarifies the sequence of the five.

The preceding serves as the cause, and the succeeding constitutes the result; therefore, faith is mentioned first, followed by wisdom at the end. Thus it is said that the former is the cause and the latter is the result.

Within the commentary, there are two parts. In explaining the first phrase, there are also three sections: first, the restatement of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*); second, the formal explanation of the text.

The meaning of explaining the powers (*bala*) after the faculties (*indriya*) by means of five or fewer [factors] is as follows: when these five factors are first established, they alternate between black and white;
at that stage, they are not yet called "powers. This is because if faith and the other [faculties] were not assisting factors, or if they were obstructed, they would be unable to function.
This is what is called the five powers (*pañcabala*). Therefore, it is said that the faculties (*indriya*) and the powers follow a sequential order.
How is it that the subsequent lines are explained below? Within this, there are also three parts: first, an inquiry; second, an answer by quoting the verse;
and third, a detailed explanation of the sequence of their arising in response to the question. The textual structure is clear.
The preceding exposition of their characteristics is now complete. As for the following sections concerning their respective stages (*bhūmi*), they likewise begin with initial arousal.

Within these two sentences, the first contrasts the preceding stage to distinguish the subsequent one; this clarifies that the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) follow the stage of liberation-aid (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

The second sentence specifically inquires regarding the location of the subsequent stage; this inquiry concerns whether the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) resides within the faculties or the powers (*bala*).
The two lines of the verse provide the direct answer. This question concerns the four stages of *uṣmagata* (heat) and so forth, which constitute the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Among these, the first two are established as faculties (*indriya*), while the latter two are described as powers (*bala*). Therefore, it is said that "the two-by-two [stages] consist of the five faculties and the five powers of the stage of penetration.

Herein, the meaning of the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) is briefly clarified. To manifest this meaning, they are analyzed through four gates: first, their names; second, their essence (*svabhāva*); third, ...

[The] Characteristics [and] the Four Stages. First, regarding the explanation of the names: the two names "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) are designated based on metaphors; the latter two are named according to their actual nature.

That is to say, when the mind of the first stage carefully contemplates the Noble Truths, it bears a resemblance to true direct realization (*abhisamaya*), much like the initial warmth produced when rubbing sticks together resembles the heat of fire at its inception. Therefore, these are named after this metaphor.

This constitutes the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). It is intended to cause the practitioner to cultivate with unremitting diligence, like one rubbing wood to produce fire, because there is not even a moment's rest.

As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, by thus contemplating the truths and having faith in them as the path to Nirvāṇa, the mind abides in a state of happiness that resembles the untainted (*anāsrava*) state.
This is called the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). It is like a person rubbing sticks together to produce fire; because one will certainly obtain the fire, it is called "Heat.

As for the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), it has the meaning of being "superior. When the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are cultivated to their highest degree, they are like the crown of a person's head—the most superior part of the body.

Therefore, based on this analogy, it is named the stage of "Summits. Just as those five powers (*pañcabala*) are of the highest degree, in terms of the Dharma, it is named the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).

1. Now, these five faculties in their superior grade are called the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) by way of metaphor. Although there are degrees of proximity [to the ultimate], they equally manifest the sense of being "superior.
As stated in the *Abhidharma*: because those Summits progress further and further and occupy a higher station; furthermore, "summit" (*mūrdhan*) carries the meaning of being "central. Why?
Because prior to the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), demerit increases while merit is slight, making spiritual cultivation difficult. Just as...

It is like ascending a mountain. After the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), evil diminishes and merit increases; thus, spiritual practice is no longer difficult, as if one were descending from a mountain.

Between these two stages, where evil and merit are equal, it is like reaching the mountain peak—having ascended but not yet descended. For this reason, based on this analogy, it is called the Stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*). As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
"Because the Stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) has progressed and evil and merit are now equal, it is named the Stage of the Summit. As [the text] says:
When a person ascends a mountain to its summit, the distance to either side is equal; thus, some say it clarifies the boundary between advancing and retreating.

Such meanings are as explained in the standard [commentaries]. The same applies to the *dharmakṣānti* (receptivity to the truths) and the *laukikāgradharma* (supreme mundane dharmas), which are also explained in the standard manner and can be understood by seeking them out.
Second, regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva*): the first two roots of goodness have the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) as their essence; the latter two...

The roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) have the five powers (*pañcabala*) as their essence. If one takes the superior concentration and wisdom as their essence, then regarding their associated factors (*sahāya*), they include all other mental states (*caitasika-dharma*), as explained in the *Abhidharma*.

As for the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage, it refers to the individual internal realization of the samādhi and prajñā of "attaining clarity" (*ālokalabdha*) regarding the various truths, along with their associated factors and so forth.
Up to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) stage, it refers to...
It is individually realized within oneself. Regarding the truths, it consists of the uninterrupted mind-samādhi and prajñā, along with their associated dharmas;
because immediately following this, one must necessarily give rise to the first supramundane path (*lokottara-mārga*). Third, regarding the analysis of its characteristics:
based on the analogy of drilling for fire, if the characteristics are analyzed separately, as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, it is like a person who wishes to...
One who wishes to produce fire by means of fire performs the following: for the sake of obtaining fire, he places dry wood below and applies a fire-drill above.
