Regarding the "stage of merit," this refers to the *saṃbhogakāya*; it is so called because it receives myriad virtues based upon the merit of myriad practices.

Regarding the "abiding in the state of affairs" (*vastu-sthiti-vastu*): this refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), which pervades the worlds of the ten directions by manifesting the eight phases of enlightenment.
These three abidings reveal the distinctions of the fruit, which are without before or after. The phrase "already explained" constitutes the third summary.
The commentary consists of three parts: first, stating the number as a general heading; second, citing the numbers for individual explanations; and third, sequentially explaining the eighteen stages.

Regarding the seventh stage, the mention of the "stage of supreme excellence" (*viśeṣa-bhūmi*) explains the word "intention" (*manas*) in the verse, because by possessing supreme excellence, one attains [powers] according to one's will.
Regarding the eighth stage, the mention of "surpassing the stages of the śrāvakas and others" refers to the presence of further increase.

Regarding the meaning of "with superior" (*sottara*): this explains the name "with superior. For a bodhisattva who has not yet entered the first stage (*bhūmi*), there is the sense that there is something superior toward which they may progress;
this explains the name "with superior. Regarding the explanation of "without superior" (*anuttara*), it is explained solely by means of one specific sense. This explains "without superior."
The remaining commentary on the text follows the previous pattern and can be understood accordingly. From "All" onwards is the third section, which provides a general summary;
it explains the passage from the verse that reads "already explained.

Below this is the second part, clarifying the stages of the *dharmadhātu*. The first line provides a general heading, while the subsequent lines provide a detailed exposition. [This refers to] the *tathatā-dharmadhātu*.

The intrinsic nature is undefiled; it is only by relying on adventitious defilements that the three stages are manifested. Therefore, it is said that the *dharmadhātu* further possesses these three [states].
As for "impure," this refers to the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), because they have not severed any of the seeds of the various afflictions (*kleśa*). As for "impure yet pure,"...
The noble stage with applied thought (*savitarka*) is so called because either cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is not yet complete or insight (*darśana*) has been completed.

That which is called "pure" (*viśuddha*) exists in the stage without applied thought (*avitarka*), because both insight and cultivation have been ultimately extinguished. The phrase "as in sequence" serves as a summary.
In the commentary, there are two parts. First, the initial phrase is explained. From "impurity" (*aśubha*) onwards, the following two phrases are explained.

Regarding the first of the four preceding stages, the three distinctions are explained in relation to the stage common to all [vehicles]. This is to demonstrate that the *dharmadhātu* is universally applicable to the three vehicles;
therefore, it is not explained by means of other categories.

Within this chapter, there are two sections. The detailed explanation of the characteristics of the stages (*avasthā*) has already been concluded above. This latter half-verse summarizes [the subject] in terms of persons (*pudgala*).
Regarding the establishment of persons herein, individuals are established according to their respective distinctions of stage;

one should understand that "according to principle" (*yathānyāyam*) is an exhortation to recognize those who establish [persons] in accordance with reason. The commentary consists of two parts; first, the general summary.

Commentary: Herein, the following sections specifically clarify the establishment of the characteristics. The phrase "abiding within the intrinsic nature" refers to the first stage, thereby clarifying the first type of person.
The phrase "this person has already entered and abided" clarifies the person established in the second stage.

Phrases such as "and so forth" serve as examples to clarify all other persons in the subsequent stages. The stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) has already been explained. What, then, are those who attain the fruit? This concludes the preceding section.
This refers to the stage after birth.

As for those who attain the fruit-stage (*phala-bhūmi*): by abiding in accordance with the previous cultivation, they manifest the characteristics of the fruit; therefore, it is called the fruit-attaining stage.
Within this chapter, there are two and a half verses divided into two sections. Two verses and one line individually manifest the characteristics of the fruits;
the final line provides a concluding summary. The first section also has two parts:

the preceding verse clarifies the five distinct fruits in relation to their causes, while the subsequent verse and line reveal the distinctions among the ten fruits according to their stages. Of these, the former...
I shall briefly clarify its meaning. The meaning of the five fruits is analyzed through three points: first, listing their names; second, clarifying their essential nature and characteristics;
and third, distinguishing them in relation to their causes. Regarding the listing of their names, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the first is the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).

Second, the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*); third, the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*); fourth, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*); and fifth, the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).

These are explained according to the general approach, wherein defiled and pure phenomena are discussed together. Now, this treatise explains them as follows: first, the "fruit of retribution" (*vipāka-phala*) is the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*);

second, the "dominant fruit" is not different from that [general] name; third, the "fruit of following the stream" (*anusrava-phala*) is the fruit of outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*); and fourth, the "fruit of effort" (*prayoga-phala*) is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

The fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is the fruit of separation (*visaṃyoga-phala*). This is explained according to a specific perspective, referring exclusively to wholesome fruits; therefore, they are presented in sequence according to their arising from the wholesome. What is this?
First, the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) induced by wholesome karma from previous lives is mentioned, because it serves as the vessel for performing wholesome deeds.

Based on the dominant power (*adhipati-bala*) of this maturation fruit, one is able to give rise to the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*); thus, the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) begins its operation.
Thereafter, because of the habitual cultivation of superior wholesome qualities in previous lives, this is the fruit of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Because of the power of one's present inclination toward these qualities, the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) reach fulfillment; this is the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*). Because they have been cultivated to perfection, one is able to abandon all hindrances;

therefore, the fifth is established as the fruit of separation (*visamyoga-phala*). Regarding the second [point], the definition of its essential nature, it is as described in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, in the chapter on the "Lineage of Powers" (*balagotra-paṭala*).

It is said: "All unwholesome dharmas receive their maturation fruit (*vipākaphala*) in the various evil destinies; wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas receive their maturation fruit in the various good destinies.
This is called the maturation fruit. Because one habituates oneself to the unwholesome, one takes pleasure in dwelling in unwholesome dharmas."

By increasing unwholesome factors and cultivating wholesome ones, one dwells happily in wholesome factors; as wholesome factors increase, the subsequent result follows in accordance with the preceding action—this is called the *niṣyanda-phala* (fruit of outflow).
The cessation of all afflictions (*kleśa*) by means of the Eightfold Noble Path is called the *visamyoga-phala* (fruit of dissociation).
If ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) cease afflictions by means of the mundane path, it is not ultimate; therefore, it is not [the fruit of] dissociation.

Regarding the result: when a certain class of persons, in the present life, exerts human effort based on any one of the various crafts or occupations—namely, agriculture, commerce, artisanship, writing, mathematics, astrology, and so forth—and thereby accomplishes results such as crops or material wealth, this is called the "result of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
If visual consciousness and so forth [arise] from the eye...
The dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) of the faculties (*indriya*) and so forth, such as sentient beings and the like, is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
If visual consciousness and so forth arise when the constituent parts of the visual faculty are neither destroyed nor dispersed, this is the dominant fruit of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

One should know that all twenty-two faculties can each give rise to their own respective dominant fruits; thus, all these are termed dominant fruits. In this context, it is said that they may resemble previous karma.

Regarding the subsequent concordant result (*niṣyanda-phala*): for example, having experienced the ripened result (*vipāka-phala*) of rebirth in the miserable realms due to taking life, one is subsequently born into the human realm and experiences the result of a short lifespan.
Likewise, having fallen into the miserable realms due to stealing, one is subsequently born among humans and experiences the result of poverty.
All such cases are subsumed under the concordant result. The rest of the text is clear; it may be understood by seeking it out. [This concludes the] essence of the five results.

The characteristics have been briefly explained in this manner. Third, regarding the classification of causes by their specific characteristics: this refers to distinguishing their differences in relation to the ten causes. The ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) is the productive cause (*ākṣepahetu*).
Among the dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*), in relation to the mind and mental factors, it is the cooperative cause (*sahabhūhetu*).

Attaining the wholesome or unwholesome is the productive cause. Attaining the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) is the originating cause (*janakahetu*). Attaining the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) is the drawing [cause].
The cause of production (*ākṣepa-hetu*): that which attains the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*) is the cause of production.

The fruits obtained from all other causes are for the most part subsumed within the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*), as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in the section on the "Ascertainment of What is Accomplished through Reflection" (*cintāmayī-viniścaya*).

Furthermore, regarding the various karmas and afflictions previously present, their ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) matures within the three realms; this ripening fruit is caused by karma and afflictions.
They are called "conditioned phenomena" (*sahetuka-dharma*) because they are the cause for the arousal of affliction.

Furthermore, the six groups of consciousness are called "conditioned phenomena" because, from the eye and forms up to the mind and mental objects, they serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) through their shared activity as causes.

Moreover, unwholesome phenomena are called "conditioned phenomena" because they are the cause for the arousal [of suffering] due to associating with evil friends, hearing what is not the true Dharma, and improper reflection. They are the opposite of these.
It should be understood that the same applies to the arising of all wholesome dharmas by way of contravening the three causes of non-arising.
Furthermore, because each of these causes possesses its own distinct dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), they are termed "dharmas with fruit.

Moreover, as long as the seeds of all dharmas—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral—have not been impaired, all those dharmas are termed [productive], because they are capable of acting as the causes for the arising and production of [their effects].
There are phenomena that possess causes. Because the arising of these causes occurs through their respective outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*), they are called phenomena that possess fruits.
Furthermore, when one dwells in a defiled state, exertion gives rise to fruitless toil and leads to a dwelling in sorrow and suffering;

whereas when one dwells in a non-defiled state, right exertion gives rise to fruitful toil and leads to a dwelling in joy and bliss. Because these [causes] function as productive causes (*ākṣepa-hetu*), they are called "possessing causes."
Regarding phenomena (*dharma*): because those very causal phenomena each possess their own individual efficient fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*), they are called "phenomena with fruit.

Furthermore, the mundane path that leads toward detachment and supramundane phenomena—which are subsumed under the noble path (*āryamārga*) and are capable of realizing *nirvāṇa*—are called "caused phenomena" (*sahetuka-dharma*) because they function as producing causes (*ākṣepaka-hetu*).
Moreover, the supramundane path is called "fruitful" because it possesses the dominant fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-adhipati-phala*).

Regarding the resultant dharmas (*phala-dharma*): these are so called by virtue of being the fruit of ultimate dissociation (*ātyantika-visaṃyoga-phala*). As for the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), it is not so by virtue of being the fruit of ultimate dissociation.
This cited passage is taken according to its thematic category; it does not necessarily follow that each point corresponds exactly to the sequence [of the original].
Such is the brief explanation of the characteristics of the five fruits.

Next, we shall correctly explain the text. Regarding the first part, the term "vessel-result" (*bhājana-phala*) refers to the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*). It is the fruit of retribution obtained through the roots of goodness cultivated in previous lives;
because one practices wholesome conduct accordingly and serves as a vessel for receiving the Path, it is called the "vessel-result.

This fruit of retribution extends across both wholesome and unwholesome realms, but here, in clarifying the "concordant result," we take up the wholesome realm. As for the term "retribution-result" (*vipāka-phala*), this refers to the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*), meaning that which is superior.

Regarding the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): because they arise through the predominant power of the retribution of the vessel-world (*bhājanavipāka*), they are designated by name according to their cause and are called "retribution fruits" (*vipākaphala*).
Next, when it says "this is the dominant fruit" (*adhipatiphala*), it is to avoid confusion with the first fruit; thus, based on its original name, it is distinguished.

While this dominant fruit applies to all phenomena, since it is established here specifically in relation to wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*), it refers exclusively to that which arises through the predominance of the retribution of the vessel-world. It says:

The "fruit of affection" (*priyaphala*) is the fruit of conformity (*nisyandaphala*). Because one has long practiced roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in previous lives, one subsequently conforms to that stream and takes delight in wholesome phenomena (*dharmas*);
thus, this fruit of conformity applies generally to all three natures (*trividha-svabhāva*). Here, however, in explaining the fruit of cultivation (*bhāvanāphala*), we take only wholesome phenomena.
As for "increase," this is the fruit of effort (*puruṣakāraphala*); because of the exertion of diligent effort in the present life, the roots of goodness increase.

"Length" refers to the fruit of fulfillment, because it is attained through perfection. The "pure fruit" is the fruit of separation (*visamyoga-phala*), because by the perfection of practice, one emerges from obstacles.
Regarding the "sequence," this refers to the establishment of the five fruits—beginning with the vessel-like fruit—in their prior and posterior order;
it is the sequence of arising based on the five fruits such as the environmental fruit (*bhājana-phala*), as they are mutually dependent.

The explanation consists of two parts. First is the explanation of the five fruits; from "this establishment" onwards is the explanation of their sequence. Regarding the "fruit of the vessel" (*bhājanaphala*):
the term "retribution" (*vipāka*) indicates the substance of the vessel, while "concomitant with the wholesome" explains the meaning of the vessel.

In the second [section], the phrase "because the fruit of the vessel is predominant" cites the causal condition that gives rise to it, which is retribution itself. "The most superior grade of wholesome roots" refers to the cause.
This clarifies the wholesome state that arises from a single cause; it correctly presents the essential nature of the fruit.

In the third [section], the phrase "because of repeated practice in previous lives" cites the preceding cause, while "delighting in wholesome dharmas" correctly presents the essential nature of the fruit. The fourth and fifth [sections] are clear in their wording and may be understood accordingly.
From this point onward, the sequential explanation provided in the commentary may likewise be understood.

Below this, the second section clarifies the ten [fruitions] by way of their stages. Within this, the first four are a brief exposition of the fruits, while the subsequent six are a detailed exposition of the fruits;
for they open up the previous four fruits by distinguishing them into six. Furthermore, the first four fruits are the progressively superior fruits (*uttarottara-phala*).

Because one anticipates the highest-highest fruit by means of the lowest-lowest causes, the latter six fruits are "conformable fruits" (*ānukūlya-phala*), established as three pairs because they correspond two by two.
Regarding the "highest-highest fruit" mentioned at the beginning, this is the first fruit; it is actually a general designation.

However, from the very beginning, a general name was established; subsequently, three distinct categories were established within that [general category]. This first fruit exists at the stage of entering practice (*pratipatti*).

Here, "entering" (*praveśa*) serves as the cause for what follows, while "practice" (*pratipatti*) serves as the entry point for what follows; viewed in relation to what precedes it, it is the fruit, and is thus termed the "superior-superior fruit" (*uttarottara-phala*).
In the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*), cultivation and abiding consist solely of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*); since one has not yet initiated the practice, no fruit is established.

That which is called the "first fruit" is actually the second fruit; because it is at the stage of attainment (*prāpti-avasthā*) that one first emerges into the supramundane, it is termed the "first fruit. As for the term "repeated practice" (*abhyāsa*):
This is the third fruit. It exists in the stage of active effort (*sābhisamskāra-avasthā*), where one advances through the cultivation of preparatory application (*prayoga*);

thus it is called the "fruit of repeated practice" (*abhyāsa-phala*). The "ultimate fruit" (*niṣṭhā-phala*) is the fourth fruit. It exists in the stage of non-abiding (*anāśrita-avasthā*) and is the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*);

therefore, it is called ultimate. The following three phrases clarify the latter six fruits. As for the term "conformity" (*anuloma*), it refers to the first of the four aforementioned superior fruits; this fruit is precisely...
This is the expedient means for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Because it accords with that [path], it is called "conforming to the fruit" (*phalānulomika*).

Among these, all three pairs are conforming; however, this general name is derived from the first one. As for "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*): this refers to the second of the four fruits mentioned previously.
Following the preceding expedient means, one first attains the path of seeing and permanently abandons the seeds or [defilements] that were previously suppressed. Therefore...

This is called the fruit of counteraction (*pratipakṣa-phala*). Regarding "separation" (*visamyoga*): among the four preceding fruits, the latter two—the fruits of the paths of training (*śaikṣa*) and beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*)—are called "separation" because they involve the separation from all hindrances and the manifestation of superior qualities (*viśeṣa-guṇa*).

As for "superior qualities," these refer to the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and so forth within those stages. By practicing in accordance with that separation from hindrances, one accomplishes these superior qualities; therefore, these two [fruits] are also [called separation].

This is in accordance [with the preceding]. The various fruits mentioned above are established based on the stage of commonality (*sādhāraṇa*). The two fruits below belong to the stage of non-commonality (*asādhāraṇa*).
Regarding the term "surpassable" (*sottara*), it refers to the Bodhisattva stages; this is explained in terms of the third stage, the stage of before and after.

Regarding the term "unsurpassable" (*anuttara*), it refers to the Tathāgata stage; this is explained in terms of the fourth stage, the stage of simultaneity. This is because the surpassable and the unsurpassable are likewise mutually concordant.
These three pairs are called the "conformable fruits" (*anuloma-phala*). The following line is the second summary. Within this explanation, there are two parts:
first, the direct explanation of the original text; second, the collective classification. Within the first part, there are also two sections.
First, there is a general outline; subsequently, the text is explained according to its sections. This section also has two parts: first, the explanation of the ten fruits;
second, the explanation of the concluding verse. Within the first part, there are also two sections: first, the direct explanation of the text; second, the analysis of the meaning.

Regarding the explanation of the text, the phrase "arising from the natural disposition" (*svabhāva-cittotpāda*) means that from the lower natural disposition, one attains the higher arising of the mind. This continues up to "the practitioner," who arises from the lower arising of the mind.

"Up to the cultivation of the higher [stages]" reveals the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the progressively superior fruits (*uttarottara-phala*). One should understand that the "successive sequence" (*paścāt-paścāt-krama*) here explains the meaning of "progressively superior" (*uttarottara*);

that is, the stage of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) is posterior to its own nature (*svabhāva*), and the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is posterior to the generation of the mind.
Based on this succession, the progressively superior fruits are established. Since the self-nature is not posterior to anything, it is not so established.
[This is] the result (*phala*). The explanation of the next three results has a textual structure that is easy to understand. Regarding the explanation of "conformity" (*anuloma*):

the phrase "because it acts as a causal condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) explains the meaning of conformity; that is, because the first result serves as the causal condition for the second result, it is called "conformity.

The phrase "one should know the superior result" indicates its essential nature (*svabhāva*). Regarding the explanation of "antidote" (*pratipakṣa*): the phrase "this is the path of cessation" (*nirodha-mārga*)...
It brings forth their essential characteristics and the path of cessation; therefore, it is called the "path of cessation. Regarding the statement that one attains the first fruit by means of this:
it is by means of this conformity that one attains the fruit of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*). This expresses the meaning of conformity in contrast to the preceding fruit.

Regarding the statement that the initial path herein is called the "fruit of counteraction" (*pratipakṣaphala*): this cites the essence of the fruit to enrich its designation. In the explanation of "separation from characteristics," the term "characteristics" [is used].
"Disjunctive fruit" (visamyoga-phala) is the citation of its name. "The fruit of repeated cultivation and the fruit of completion" is the statement of its essence;
that is to say, among the four preceding fruits, the latter two constitute its essence, because "completion" (pariniṣpanna) carries the meaning of "ultimate" (niṣṭhā).

"In order to distance oneself from, or to abandon, the hindrances" explains the meaning of disjunction (visamyoga). "Like the fruits of the various noble ones, both those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), in their respective order" [is the further clarification].
This is an explanation of their resultant stages (*phala-avasthā*) by way of the individuals [who attain them]. The textual structure for the explanation of the next three results is clear.
The passage beginning with "In this way" further differentiates these meanings. Regarding the statement "these four results": first, the fourth is called the ultimate result (*niṣṭhā-phala*);
second, the seventh is called the result of separation (*visamyoga-phala*); third, the eighth is called the result of the superior stage (*viśeṣa-avasthā-phala*); and fourth, the tenth is called...

The unsurpassed fruit. These four kinds of fruits all manifest the distinctions within the state of the perfected fruit; therefore, it is said they are for the purpose of distinguishing the perfected fruit.
Based on this, one should understand the remaining six fruits as being for the purpose of distinguishing the causes, though they are not explicitly mentioned here.

They are not mentioned because they do not function in the same way. This is because the four fruits equally manifest the fruit of a single stage, whereas the six fruits follow [the distinctions of the stages].
Because it reveals the causes for the distinct stages, the following brief explanation serves to interpret its concluding statement.

The phrase "to briefly state such a multitude" is the actual commentary on the text; it is called "multitude" because there are either five or ten [categories]. The phrase "if explained extensively, they are immeasurable" clarifies the intent of the conclusion.
That is to say, the meaning of the concluding statement "briefly stated" is intended to show that an extensive explanation would be immeasurable.
This is the fruit.
The first section above, the direct explanation of the text, is now complete. From here below is the second section, the general collection and analysis, which contains two parts:

first, the actual collection of meanings; second, the conclusion of the ultimate. Within the first part, there are three sections: first, the collection of antidotes; next, the collection of cultivation...

[The stage of] attainment. Subsequently, one gathers [the conditions] to realize the fruit. This [process] also has two parts: the general indication and the specific gathering. Within the specific gathering, in contrast to the superior grade, twelve types of cultivation are enumerated.
Regarding "cultivation of awakening," this refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*), for it is free from ignorance (*avidyā*).

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* calls this "cultivation of manifestation" (*saṃdarśana-bhāvanā*), because it removes the darkness of ignorance and clearly illuminates the objects of cognition. It causes [defilements] to become thin through cultivation.

These are the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*). Because one diligently cultivates two kinds of goodness and attenuates two kinds of evil, that treatise calls this "cultivation of diminution and destruction" (*apacaya-bhāvanā*).

As for "cultivation of mastery" (*parikarma-bhāvanā*), it refers to the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); since their essence is meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and they accomplish the path of mastery, that treatise calls this "cultivation of mastery through accomplishment.
"Cultivation of superior states" refers to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), which serve to give rise to the higher stages; [the next stage] is the five powers (*pañcabala*).

Because it is capable of accomplishing the task, that treatise calls it "cultivation of subsequent practice" (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-bhāvanā*). "Cultivation of secret union" refers to the five powers (*pañcabala*);
because practice accords with principle and is able to overcome the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said that "wisdom reaches the object as one family," which explains the meaning of "secret union."
That treatise calls this "cultivation of correspondence" (*yoga-bhāvanā*). As for "superior cultivation," it refers to the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*);

because they first enter the supramundane and transcend the mundane, that treatise calls this "cultivation of supreme knowledge" (*jñāna-viśeṣa-bhāvanā*). As for "excellent cultivation," it refers to the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*);

because one enters the cultivation of the path and excels even the superior [stage], that treatise calls this "supreme-of-the-supreme cultivation" (*uttarottara-bhāvanā*). This is the initial setting forth.

"Cultivation of the initial stage" refers to the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). As the preceding verse states: "Because there is delusion following non-delusion. That treatise calls this "cultivation of the initial limit" (*pūrvānta-bhāvanā*).
"Cultivation of the middle stage" refers to the level of noble ones in training (*śaikṣa*). As the preceding verse states: "Because there is non-delusion following delusion.

That treatise calls this "cultivation of the middle limit" (*madhyānta-bhāvanā*). "Cultivation of the final stage" refers to the level of noble ones beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). As stated previously..."
The verse states: "Because it is non-erroneous and free from following error. That treatise calls this the "cultivation of the final limit" (*paryanta-bhāvanā*).

"Cultivation with superior" refers to the cultivation of the two vehicles; "unexcelled cultivation" refers to the cultivation of the Bodhisattvas. As the preceding verse stated, there are distinctions in terms of "object," "contemplation," and "attainment.
By citing these three meanings—namely, that the object has no superior and is not inferior—the verse explains what is "unexcelled."

Furthermore, regarding the statement "there is no accumulation," the Bodhisattva contemplates and deconstructs all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), practicing non-apprehension; therefore, it is said there is no accumulation.
This is in contrast to the contemplation of the Two Vehicles, who conceive of marks such as accumulation, suffering, and impermanence.

The following is the second section, concerning the meaning of the stage of "cultivation through accumulation" (*saṃbhāra-bhāvanā-vihāra*). This section also has two parts: a general heading and a detailed explanation.

Briefly stated, there are five stages that collectively constitute the various dwellings of cultivation. Regarding the first point, the phrase "one should achieve the dwelling of cultivation" cites its name.

The statement "this person dwells within their own nature" identifies the person as belonging to a specific stage; this refers to the aforementioned name. Although one has not yet perfected the dwelling of cultivation by means of the causal dwelling, [the name is applied].

Because it possesses the nature of what is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is called "that which is to be accomplished" (*sādhya*). In the second [section], the phrase "performing activities, cultivation, and abiding" cites the name [of that stage];

the subsequent mention of "the generation of the mind" up to "the practitioner" corresponds to its respective positions—namely, the aforementioned names for the "stage of entry" and the "stage of practice.
In the third [section], the phrase "named the stage of supreme purity" first cites the preceding stage; that is to say, the previous [first]...
The fourth is the stage of attainment (*prāpti*). The name "attainment" is identical to the stage of the *dharmakāya*; therefore, it is called the "most pure stage.
As for the subsequent mention of the "most pure stage," this establishes its designation;

it indicates that while this stage is not most pure in essence, it is so designated as being "most pure," and is thus called the "abode of the most pure. Regarding the statement in the fourth [section] concerning "dwelling in the stage of adornment," this is...
"Establishing its name as 'pervading the ten stages' (*daśabhūmiparipūrṇa*) explains the meaning of 'ornamentation.

Within the ten others, the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*), the ten perfections (*pāramitā*), and so forth—the conditioned and unconditioned qualities—are all-pervasive; therefore, it is called the stage of cultivation and abiding with ornamentation (*sālaṃkārabhāvanāvihāra*).
Regarding the statement in the fifth [chapter] that it is the 'unexcelled stage of abiding,' this establishes its name, while the meaning has already been clarified previously."

Therefore, they are not explained further. By means of these five stages, one should understand that the eighteen types of stages mentioned above, as well as the three stages of the dharma-dhātu to be explained next, are subsumed within them as appropriate.

The third section below concerns the meaning of the "collection" (*saṃgraha*) of these fruits. This section also has two parts: a general heading and a detailed classification. Within the detailed classification, six kinds of fruits are clarified;
first their names are listed, and subsequently their characteristics are analyzed. First, regarding the "fruit of inclusion" (*parigraha-phala*): it collects the five preceding fruits.

Among those five fruits—such as the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) and so forth—it includes all fruits without exception. Furthermore, it includes the "fruit of the vessel" (*bhājana-phala*) and the others.
All [the fruits] are subsumed within the five fruits, as ten types of fruits are subsequently explained. For these two reasons, they are called the "fruits of inclusion.

Second, regarding the "most excellent fruits": by gathering those ten fruits and situating them within the universal inclusion of the five fruits, one selects the most excellent among them to establish these ten fruits;
therefore, they are named the "most excellent fruits. The subsequent two fruits further clarify the five fruits.

The latter two fruits further clarify the ten fruits. Third, the fruit of repeated cultivation (*abhyāsa-phala*) clarifies the first of the five fruits, the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), because it is the retribution obtained from repeatedly cultivating roots of goodness.
Fourth, the fruit of successive superior extraction (*uttarottara-niṣyanda-phala*) clarifies the latter four fruits within the five fruits;

it refers to the extraction of the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) upon the basis of the fruit of maturation, and so on, up to the extraction [of the fruit] upon the basis of the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Because it produces the fruit of separation from [defilements]. Fifth, the "concise fruit" (*saṃkṣipta-phala*) indicates the first four fruits among the ten.
Sixth, the "extensive fruit" (*vistara-phala*) indicates the latter six fruits among the ten. The meaning of concise and extensive has already been explained previously.

Herein, the characteristics are indicated in sequence as follows: the statement that "the fruit of maintenance (*parigraha-phala*) consists of five kinds of fruits" clarifies the meaning of the first fruit.
As stated previously, the phrase "the remaining fruits are the five distinct fruits" indicates the most preeminent fruit.
The ten fruits mentioned later are called "remaining fruits" because they are the most distinguished among the five fruits; thus, they are referred to as the distinct fruits of those five.

The statement that "it is called the fruit of retribution (vipākaphala) because it was accumulated in previous lives" indicates the fruit of repeated practice (*abhyāsa-phala*). Among the five fruits...

Regarding the initial statement, "Because the supreme-superior [attainment] is drawn forth, there are four kinds of fruits," this refers to the fruit drawn forth by the supreme-superior, which consists of the latter four among the five.
Regarding the statement, "If briefly stated, the supreme-superior fruit has four kinds," this reveals the abbreviated fruits;
these are the first four fruits among the ten, as they are explained according to their general meaning. Thus, it is said that the supreme-superior fruit has four kinds.
This refers to the "types. To say that, if explained extensively, there are six types of concordant fruits (*anuloma-phala*) is to reveal the extensive fruits;
these are the latter six among the ten fruits. Furthermore, this is stated according to the general sense, hence it is said that there are six concordant fruits.

The phrase "because these four kinds of fruits are explained in detail through their differentiation" explains the term "extensive fruits" (*vipula-phala*); it means that based on the preceding four fruits, six are explained through their differentiation. Therefore, [the latter...]
The six kinds are called the "Extensive Fruit" (*vipulaphala*).

From the "Middle and Extremes" (*madhyānta*) onwards, this concludes the ultimate [teaching]. Regarding the statement that "there are four places here," speaking in terms of general characteristics, the three categories of counteractive cultivation (*pratipakṣabhāvanā*), abiding (*sthiti*), and attainment of fruit (*phalaprāpti*) are combined into a single place.
This is because stages (*avasthā*) are established based on practice, and fruits (*phala*) are established based on those stages. Thus says the text.

Because their momentum is mutually reinforced and there is no separation between them, the Master of the Commentary (*Śāstrakāra*) combines these three categories into a single location for the sake of unifying their meaning.
For this reason, when one arrives at this point, there are four locations: first, characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); second, obscurations (*āvaraṇa*); third, reality (*tattva*);

and the fourth, which refers to the fruit of practice and abiding (*caryā-sthiti-phala*). Therefore, it is said that there are four [locations] here; within the fourth location, there are further subdivisions.
Because three meanings are established as separate chapters, they are called "three sections.
